19750-the-waif-woman:
Robert Louis Stevenson set The Waif Woman in old Norse Iceland. Finnward is a prosperous man who keeps open house. His wife Aud cares more for fine clothes and admiration. She is thought careless in her conduct for a married woman. Their children are Eyolf, a likely boy, and Asdis, a young daughter. Trouble is plainly gathering around the household.

Stevenson loved saga style: flat telling, heavy fate. A waif woman, a castaway stranger, brings the outside world into Finnward's hall. Stevenson's Norse tales show his range beyond Treasure Island. He retells northern material in spare, hard prose. The story stays little known, which makes it a find. It shows a master storyteller testing an ancient form.
19833-the-heroic-enthusiasts-gli-eroici-:
Part the second of Giordano Bruno's Heroic Enthusiasts continues his dialogues on heroic love. Its pages play with the number nine, ninth letter and ninth door. Fifty portals, it says, lead to the concealed mysteries of being. Od is named the pure life-giving light, or magnetic fluid. Bruno's text, in this edition, wears layers of mystical commentary. The result is heady and strange.

Victorian occult interest revived Bruno as a martyr of free thought. Editions like this one fed that revival. The commentary's talk of Od comes from Baron von Reichenbach's magnetism theories. Bruno's own sonnets and arguments sit beneath the gloss. Readers must dig for the philosopher under the mystic. Part two rewards that digging.
19863-the-old-masters-and-their-pictures:
Sarah Tytler wrote The Old Masters and Their Pictures for the use of schools. Her survey gives many records of Dutch painters in particular. Dutch art, she notes, proved specially popular in England. Some Dutch masters are better represented in England than at home. Flemish art also gets full treatment here. J. A. Crowe revised the art history for this edition.

School art history began with books like this one. Pupils learned painters' lives beside their famous pictures. The canon here is the Victorian canon: Raphael to Rembrandt. Tytler writes clearly for young students without flattening the art. Her selections shaped what schoolchildren thought great painting was. The book documents that teaching tradition well.
19988-little-maid-marian:
Amy E. Blanchard wrote Little Maid Marian in 1908, a story for girls. Marian talks often with her grandmother in its pages. Faith, both feel, is difficult to exercise completely. Marian has made numberless mighty efforts to believe as she should. Yet things did not come out as her efforts promised. The gap between effort and outcome troubles her young conscience. Blanchard writes that trouble gently.

Blanchard's girls' books often carry quiet religious feeling. Marian's doubts are treated as growth, not failure. Grandmother and granddaughter anchor the story's warmth. The setting is a modest, churchgoing American household. Young readers got companionship for their own questions. The book is a soft-spoken period piece for girls.
20132-the-wizard-of-the-sea-or-a-trip-un:
Roy Rockwood wrote The Wizard of the Sea, a trip under the ocean for boys. Young Mont hears he may join a nautical school with a sly grin. A town man calls him the worst boy in town for mischief. Mont takes the charge with more pride than shame, it seems.

Rockwood wrote many sea and adventure tales under that shared name. A school at sea leads, here, to a craft that dives below waves. Undersea travel was still a marvel when the book came out. Readers get boyish fun mixed with wonder at a new kind of ship.
20205-the-maya-chronicles-brinton-s-libr:
The Maya Chronicles gathers native Maya texts in Daniel Brinton's library series. Brinton sought true specimens of native literature for American scholars. Such works are rare and hard to reach, he warns readers. They sit in manuscript with a few collectors, or in costly society volumes.

This volume brings Maya chronicles from Yucatan into print for study. They record kings, wars, famines, and the coming of the Spanish. Brinton's series aimed to save aboriginal American literature from loss. Readers get primary Maya history in translation, with a scholar's care around it.
20279-the-veterinarian:
The Veterinarian is a reference book for those who treat sick and hurt animals. One entry defines creosote, a colorless to yellowish oily liquid. It holds phenols and comes from the destructive distillation of wood tar. Beech wood tar, in particular, yields much of the supply described.

Creosote once served as a medicine for chronic bronchitis in practice. Entries like this one give drugs, doses, and uses in plain order. Farmers and vets kept such books close in stable and surgery. Readers get a practical window on animal medicine of an earlier age.
20439-susan-b-anthony-rebel-crusader-hum:
Alma Lutz wrote this life of Susan B. Anthony, published by Beacon Press in 1959. Its subtitle calls Anthony a rebel, a crusader, and a humanitarian. Lutz had spent years gathering letters and records of the women's rights movement.

Anthony spent her long life fighting for women's right to vote. She spoke, organized, and faced arrest for casting a ballot in 1872. The biography follows her from her Quaker childhood to national fame. It remains a standard life of the leader who did more than any other to win American women the vote.
20555-what-is-and-what-might-be-a-study-:
What Is and What Might Be studies education in general and elementary education in particular. Its author was a school inspector who came to doubt the cramming system of his day. The book argues that schools crush the very powers they claim to train.

Our faculties grow by use, the book holds. Once they reach their fullest growth, we keep them at that level by exercising them. Mental and spiritual powers have no fixed limit, so the need for exercise is more urgent still. To neglect them is to stunt them. The study became a noted plea for freer, fuller schooling.
20754-the-blunders-of-a-bashful-man:
Shyness is the curse of the man who tells The Blunders of a Bashful Man. He hopes no other soul must bear the mishaps his complaint has cost him. Smallpox and scarlet fever, he notes, strike once, but bashfulness strikes for life.

Comic scenes pile up as the poor man trips through calls, meals, and courtship. Each fresh crowd brings a fresh blunder to dread. The humor is gentle, built on pain most readers know at least a little. This slight, funny book shows how Victorian humor could turn a common flaw into a whole tale of woe.
21063-the-missing-merchantman:
Harry Collingwood worked as a ship designer and shipwright, and that trade knowledge runs through this sea novel. The crew of a merchant vessel decide that captains and officers are paid far too much. Convinced they have been robbed of fair wages for years, the deckhands seize the ship.

In taking the vessel the crew make themselves little better than pirates. The officers and passengers, though, are resourceful people who work their way out of the trap. At last they bring their ship home, where she has long been posted as missing. The tale mixes mutiny, seamanship, and a sharp argument about pay and skill.
21065-the-log-of-a-privateersman:
Early in the nineteenth century, with Britain at war against France, privateers worked as licensed sea raiders against enemy shipping. Harry Collingwood's novel opens with a bold French stroke in October 1804. French sailors slip into Weymouth harbour at night and carry off the trader Weymouth, loaded with rum, sugar, and tobacco.

From that capture the hero's career as a privateersman grows. He proves very good at preying on enemy ships and taking prizes. His success at last brings him an offer of a permanent commission in the Royal Navy. The log form keeps the action close to decks, watches, and pay-offs.
21331-the-adventures-of-hajji-baba-of-is:
James Morier's comic novel follows Hajji Baba, a Persian barber's son, through every trade and scrape his country offers. Chapter headings tell the pattern. He is captured by Turcomans, rescues his master's money and keeps it, and becomes a robber in self-defence. Later he works as a water carrier and an itinerant seller of smoke.

Morier had lived in Persia as a British diplomat, and the tale pokes fun at Persian manners and English ones alike. The poet Asker's history and the dervish Sefer's story fill side chapters. George Curzon introduced this 1895 edition. Hajji Baba remains the classic English comic novel of Persia, sharp, episodic, and often unfair in the way of good satire.
21415-the-young-visiters-or-mr-salteena-:
Daisy Ashford wrote The Young Visiters as a child, and it reached print in 1919 with a preface by J. M. Barrie. Mr Salteena, a man of forty-two, loves having guests to stay. His young guest Ethel Monticue, aged seventeen, joins him at the start.

Ashford keeps her child spelling and her grave, funny view of grown-up life. Visits, a trip to the Crystal Palace, grand calls, and a proposal fill the short tale. A wedding brings the plot to its close. The book became a famed curio, loved for the clear young voice that never slips.
21532-the-university-of-michigan:
Wilfred Shaw, the university's alumni chief, wrote The University of Michigan in 1920. Shaw edited the Michigan Alumnus and etched four of the book's pictures himself. Photographs crowd the rest of the volume, from University Hall onward.

Chapters run from the founding and early days to Presidents Angell and Hutchins. Schools of law, medicine, and letters get their own accounts. Student life, fraternities, athletics, and town and campus fill later pages. A chapter on the university in war, and one on its alumni, close the tale. The odd first name of the school, the Catholepistemiad, gets its due at the start.
21576-the-privateersman:
A cruise off Hispaniola in the privateer Revenge opens Captain Marryat's The Privateersman, published in 1846. The narrator hopes his tale, if ever made public, may bring profit to its readers. Privateering, as Marryat notes, is piracy made lawful by a government's licence.

The Revenge takes a French ship early, then holds her course for more prizes. Marryat's twenty-third book draws on the last great age of the privateer. Captures, fights, and the division of prize money fill the log-like tale. No writer knew this world better from the inside than a post-captain turned novelist.
21582-the-mightiest-man:
Patrick Fahy's tale The Mightiest Man, from Worlds of If in November 1961, opens after aliens have left Earth. A few shining metal huts in the Siberian tundra alone prove they came. Earth stood helpless while vast minds slithered over her fields and cities.

They caught up with the mightiest man in Belgrade, the blurb declares, and he feared nothing. A neural plague has spread to Zagreb, Albania, and Italy in the tale's grim reach. Twenty million lunatics fill the Balkans, and the Danube stands dammed into a lake. Fahy asks who betrayed mankind, and at what price, in a stark cold-war nightmare.
21700-don-juan:
Lord Byron turns the Don Juan legend inside out in Don Juan, his great comic epic in verse. The poem runs to seventeen cantos in the copy given here, with a sharp dedication. Juan is no bold seducer here, but a young man whom women pursue.

Byron opens fire on Southey, the poet laureate, and the Lake poets at Keswick. Their narrow circle, he charges, thinks poetry's wreaths belong to them alone. Shipwreck, a slave market, a sultan's court, and the siege of Ismail fill the cantos. Love affairs, war, and English society all take Byron's wit in ottava rima, the poem's dancing, rhyming measure.
21719-blue-lights-hot-work-in-the-soudan:
Miles Milton stands at a turning point in his life as this Ballantyne novel opens. Ballantyne compares him to water at a ridge, where one drop flows to the Atlantic and the next to Hudson's Bay. Miles leans the wrong way, and the book follows where that false step leads. His strong will and hot temper keep causing trouble at home.

The trail leads at last to the Soudan, where British troops fought in desert heat. Ballantyne mixes a young man's moral fall and recovery with scenes of real campaigning. The title's blue lights point to the Christian soldiers whose faith lights the darker parts of the tale.
21743-jeff-benson-or-the-young-coastguar:
Jeff Benson loses his father, a poor schoolmaster in the coastal town of Cranby, as this Ballantyne tale opens. Jeff is fifteen, tall, hearty, and sure he can do anything he sets his mind to. Fun has ruled his life so far, in school and on the playground. His uncle Jacob, a hard and grasping lawyer, cares little for the boy.

Work by the sea gives Jeff his chance, and the coastguard gives him his calling. Ballantyne follows the lad from schoolboy pranks to rescues on a dangerous coast. Smugglers, storms, and duty test the young coastguardsman in turn. It is a steady tale of a boy growing straight under hard knocks and salt air.
21962-harvard-classics-volume-28-essays-:
Great essays in English fill this twenty-eighth volume of the Harvard Classics, Dr. Charles W. Eliot's famous five-foot shelf of books, issued in 1910. The frontispiece shows Thomas Huxley, whose Science and Culture stands inside. Swift and Thackeray open the prose line. Newman's lectures on the idea of a university follow, with his account of university life at Athens.

Matthew Arnold's Study of Poetry and Ruskin's Sesame and Lilies carry the Victorian center. Milton, Bagehot, Freeman on race and language, Pepys on truth of intercourse, and Stevenson close the range. Introductions and notes frame each author. The volume is a portable university of English prose, chosen to prove that a busy reader could self-educate from a single shelf.
21997-christie-s-old-organ:
An old barrel-organ man and a lost boy meet in O. F. Walton's Christie's Old Organ, also called Home, Sweet Home. Old Treffy sits alone in his attic in a dreary lodging house, turning his organ with a trembling hand. The tune it plays, Home Sweet Home, mocks every bare bench below. Yet the flowers of love still live in his withered heart, and he gives them all to his antiquated organ.

Walton wrote tales for Sunday school readers, and this is among her best known. Christie, the boy of the story, learns what home means from the old man who has none. The clergyman pictured with Christie carries the tale's gentle preaching. Sentimental in the Victorian way, the little book moved generations of young readers.
22072-folk-lore-and-legends-north-americ:
Folk-Lore and Legends: North American Indian gathers tales told by Native peoples across the continent. The volume belongs to a popular series that sorted old stories by the peoples who told them. One tale concerns a village belle admired by every hunter and warrior. Her suitor, the Beau-Man, trusts his secrets to a friend, and trouble follows.

Other stories tell of spirits, animals, courtship, and revenge in the woods and villages. The tellers' names and tribes stand behind many of the pieces. Such collections preserved tales that might otherwise have stayed only in oral tradition. They also show how nineteenth-century readers liked their folklore: romantic, brief, and framed as a window on a vanishing world.
22073-the-repairman:
Harry Harrison wrote The Repairman, a short science fiction tale from the early days of his career. Harrison later became famous for the Stainless Steel Rat books and Make Room! Make Room! His repairman narrator has fixed hyperspace beacons across the whole Galaxy. He boasts that he has worked on every type or model ever made.

Then a call names a kind of beacon he has never heard of. The job takes him somewhere stranger than his long experience prepared him for. Harrison builds the joke and the puzzle out of one man's professional pride. The story is quick, dry, and typical of the clever short fiction that filled the science fiction magazines of the 1950s.
22140-the-wrong-woman:
Charles D. Stewart published The Wrong Woman in 1912, a novel of the American West. The frontispiece shows a woman who must continue her journey afoot. Stewart opens on ranch matters: a horse that swells itself out when saddled, then lets the girths hang loose. Such stable talk sets the scene among people who live by horses.

A case of mistaken identity drives the plot, as the title promises. The wrong woman arrives where another was expected, and ranch life must sort out the error. Stewart writes comedy and courtship in a Western setting. His books were known for shrewd humour about human nature, and this one keeps that reputation.
22182-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-v:
Volume V of The Best of the World's Classics turns to Great Britain and presents its prose masters. The set was a standard home library of its day, ten volumes strong. Each author arrives with a short life. Boswell's sketch, for example, runs from his birth in 1740 to his Life of Johnson in 1791 in a few brisk lines.

Essays, speeches, and passages from the great prose writers fill the volume. The editors chose what a general reader was expected to know. Such collections built the canon for homes without a scholar's library. This volume shows Edwardian taste in British prose: Johnson's circle, the essayists, and the historians, all in one thick book.
22331-the-chocolate-soldier-or-heroism-t:
C. T. Studd wrote The Chocolate Soldier, a sharp call for braver Christians. Its full title calls heroism the lost chord of Christianity. Studd mocks soft believers with his chocolate soldier figure.

The Chocolate Christian, he writes, shakes at the very thought of war. The call to battle always finds him with the palsy. Such a man says he cannot move, only sing. Studd quotes the man's favorite lines without mercy. The pamphlet argues that faith should produce courage and sacrifice. It still reads as a brisk, stinging challenge. Studd wanted soldiers for Christ, not sweets that melt when heat comes.
22371-the-chief-end-of-man:
The Chief End of Man, dated 1897, takes up life's largest question directly. Its title echoes the old catechism answer about man's purpose. The passage preserved shows a man in deep perplexity, near dismay.

At such a time, the writer counsels looking backward attentively. A guided life can review the steps by which it advanced. Past crises, once recalled, show how they were met. Light may then break on the path ahead. Or the reader may simply take fresh heart and hope. The book offers that counsel at length. It treats purpose as something proved by a whole life's road.
22532-mary-louise-and-josie-o-gorman:
Edith Van Dyne wrote Mary Louise and Josie O'Gorman, published in 1922. Van Dyne was a pen name used for popular girls' series books. Hard news opens this volume for Mary Louise and her friends.

Hope of Danny Dexter's survival was finally abandoned by everyone. His sorrowing little wife and many friends gave up that hope. Colonel Hathaway's comfortable fortune had also mysteriously disappeared by then. Mary Louise thus faced a future of poverty without warning. With native pluck, she rose to the sad occasion bravely. In spite of her sad heart, she showed cheerful spirit. Josie O'Gorman, girl detective, helps drive the mystery plot. Readers get series fiction with courage under loss.
22664-the-severed-hand-from-german-tales:
Wilhelm Hauff wrote The Severed Hand, a dark tale from his fairy-tale almanacs, here taken from German Tales as published for American readers. The catalog record gives no year. Hauff, who died young, filled his brief career with stories of the East, of students, and of quiet horror.

The sample opens in farewell: a father embraces his son and gives him clothes for the journey, plus the weapons his grandfather hung on the father when he went abroad. Use them only when attacked, the father counsels, but then defend yourself bravely. Such blessings arm the hero for a tale of murder, disguise, and a hand that will not rest. Hauff mixes the storyteller's ease with real dread, and this is among his most gripping tales.
22840-honor-o-callaghan:
Schoolgirl rank is serious business in Honor O'Callaghan, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. The excerpt looks inside a fashionable house of education, where a newcomer's place turns on odd details. One mother calls on her daughter attended by only one footman, and the slight is noted. A father's town address and a mother's milliner also weigh in the scale.

Mitford watches this small world with amused precision. Honor, the Irish girl of the title, must make her way among classmates quick to judge surfaces. The story turns school etiquette into a study of class itself. Beneath the manners sits a real question about worth. The tale answers it the Mitford way, through character shown in daily behavior.
22844-miss-philly-firkin-the-china-woman:
A crowded London street opens Miss Philly Firkin, the China Woman, by Mary Russell Mitford. Houses in the best streets let for double their value, goods sell at nearly the same rate, and horse traffic and foot traffic jostle on the pavement. Coaches and phaetons run against each other in the road.

Philly Firkin keeps her china shop inside that crush of commerce. Mitford follows the small tradeswoman through the risks and pleasures of city shopkeeping, where a fragile stock meets a rough crowd. The portrait mixes sympathy with sharp observation of London manners. Village readers of Mitford's sketches got a capital-city counterpart here. Philly's counter becomes a fine post from which to watch the whole town go by.
23152-the-mcbrides-a-romance-of-arran:
John Sillars lays out his chapters in The McBrides, a romance of Arran. Chapter titles promise the Urie's foot as a resting place, a halflin's message, and another ride to McAllan's locker. A doorstep wedding, a kiss from Margaret McBride, Betty's growing pains, and a raking black schooner fill out the list.

Arran, the Firth of Clyde island called Scotland in miniature, frames the McBrides' fortunes. Smuggling schooners, weddings, and messages cross the island's hills in Sillars's Highland manner. The chapter heads alone tell a family saga's rhythm, rest, errands, weddings, and sails on the horizon. Readers who enjoy Scottish regional romance, dialect and all, will find a whole island community between these covers, arranged around one family's name.
23191-count-ulrich-of-lindburg-a-tale-of:
Count Ulrich of Lindburg is a tale of the Reformation in Germany. Its scene is the Castle of Lindburg, on the banks of the river Saal at Merseburg in Saxony. The land then answered to the aged Elector Frederick, praised in the tale as an excellent ruler.

The castle is drawn as a feudal pile from the Middle Ages, proof against the siege tools of older war. Yet such strongholds were bound to crumble before cannon fire. The tale links that fall to a wider change: the old order giving way before the light of Gospel truth.
23194-the-common-man: Guy McCord's The Common Man opens on a small, telling gesture. A man named Braun lets a sentence trail off, then stuffs a paper into a coat pocket that has clearly served as a waste bin for years. He leads the way up a cement walk, with his younger companions close behind him.
23245-ancient-ballads-and-legends-of-hin:
Ancient Ballads and Legends of Hindustan gathers poems retelling old Indian stories. Its introduction tells a sad, striking story about the poet herself. Within four years of her death, it says, her genius had been revealed to the world in many forms and recognised across France and England.

At her death she had published only one book. That book had found only two reviewers in Europe. The gap between those two facts gives the volume its charge. Readers get ballads and legends from a young Indian poet whose name, the editor insists, no well-read person should fail to know.
23269-the-heir-of-kilfinnan-a-tale-of-th:
The Heir of Kilfinnan is a tale of the shore and ocean, told here through a later summary of its plot. After several exciting events, an earl dies. To everyone's surprise, the young hero Denham is revealed as Dermot, a young man met much earlier in the tale.

A lawyer then states that Dermot's father stood in line to the earldom. That makes Dermot the new earl, and the room erupts in cheers. One catch remains: who wants a ruined castle and a bankrupt estate? Readers get inheritance, hidden identity, and sea adventure in a cheerfully spoiled package.
23270-on-the-indian-trail-stories-of-mis:
On the Indian Trail gathers stories of missionary work among Cree and other Indigenous peoples. Its author explains the book's shape at the start. Unlike some of his other books, it is not one continuous narrative of missionary life, but a set of distinct chapters.

Some chapters were written just for this volume. Others had already seen print, in whole or in part, and are gathered here at the request of friends, with the publishers' courtesy. Readers get first-hand period accounts of travel, teaching, and mission stations, told as separate episodes rather than one long story.
a-mountain-woman:
Elia Wilkinson Peattie gathers tales of the American West, most first printed in magazines such as Harper's Weekly and the Cosmopolitan, as her foreword notes. The title story opens with a letter from Colorado: the writer has married a mountain woman, a remnant, he says, of the heroic ages. Eight tales follow, including Jim Lancy's Waterloo and The Three Johns.

Her people are miners, ranch families, schoolteachers, and wanderers in Colorado, Michigan, and the gulches. Peattie writes women who endure weather, loss, and rough men without losing warmth or humor. The tales mix dialect, landscape, and sentiment in the regional style her day loved, and they keep a clear eye on frontier hardship.
a-new-voyage-to-carolina-containing-the-:
John Lawson, surveyor-general of North Carolina, published his voyage account in the early seventeen hundreds, and the title page promises an exact description and natural history of the country. The first part reports his journal of a thousand miles traveled through several nations of Indians. Lawson writes as an explorer who walked the ground himself.

He describes rivers, soil, plants, beasts, and fish, then the customs, dress, food, wars, and beliefs of the native peoples he met. The second part gives the present state of the colony, its towns, trade, and prospects for settlers. Lawson's plain, curious record remains a key source for the early Carolina backcountry and its peoples.
a-people-s-man:
A People's Man is a 1914 political novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, who called himself the prince of storytellers. Oppenheim wrote some one hundred fifty novels, mainly of suspense and international intrigue. He was among the earliest writers of modern spy fiction and founded the rogue male school of adventure thrillers, and this book turns his hand to politics at home.

As its title signals, the story follows a man of the people through the world of Westminster power. Ambition, loyalty, and public pressure collide in the Edwardian political scene. The novel shows Oppenheim applying his thriller pace to Parliament and party struggle, rather than to the foreign intrigue of his better-known tales.
a-poor-wise-man:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens in a steel city seen from the railway, blackened walls and river mist under a gray, smoke-laden sky. Through its gates come hopeful workers and men who would destroy their dreams. After the Great War, the city simmers with strikes, radicals, and fear.

Fifty-two chapters follow a rich steel family, its rebellious daughter, and Willy Cameron, the poor wise man of the title, a clerk whose plain decency steadies everyone he touches. Rinehart mixes romance with a serious look at labor unrest and revolutionary plots in America. Known for mysteries, she here writes a novel of ideas about class, loyalty, and the country's future.
adventures-in-the-land-of-canaan:
Robert Lee Berry says in his foreword that his book comes out of his heart and is meant for the hearts of others. Some of it was learned by long and bitter experience. His introductory chapter explains the plan: Israel's story, from bondage in Egypt to conquering Canaan, is a type of the Christian's path from sin to entire sanctification.

Thirteen chapters follow that path as a pilgrimage. They cover getting ready to enter, crossing the Jordan, and a memorial stone. They explore Canaan by faith. They fight Giant Accuser, Giant Mistake, and Giant Doubt. They enter the dungeon of Giant Discourager. The wine of prayer and the pilgrims of the victorious life close the course. Berry writes holiness teaching as allegory, in Bunyan's long shadow.
an-amiable-charlatan: An Amiable Charlatan is a 1916 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, the English master of suspense and international intrigue. By this date Oppenheim was a major popular author, midway through a career of some one hundred fifty novels. The story centers on its title figure, a charming rogue whose schemes drive the tale, in the light, plot-led style that made Oppenheim a household name for thriller readers of his era.
an-iceland-fisherman:
Pierre Loti writes of the Breton fishermen who sail each year to fish off Iceland, in M. Jules Cambon's translation. A long prefatory essay praises Loti's power to carry readers into far lands with simple art. The novel itself divides between the icy sea and the Breton land, as its part titles state.

On the Iceland grounds the men work through fog and storm while the women wait at home in Brittany. A first love grows between a fisherman and a girl of his village, shadowed by orders for foreign service and the sea's long record of taking men. Loti keeps the plot spare and the feeling deep, and the ending is among the saddest in French fiction.
another-study-of-woman:
Honoré de Balzac sets his tale at a Paris ball, in a translation by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell. When the glittering party thins out, a smaller circle stays behind for the real talk of the night. There the company falls to discussing women, marriage, and love, and one guest tells a story to prove his point.

The frame lets Balzac stage a contest of wits among fashionable men and women, each with a theory and a past. A tale within the tale, of a woman's sacrifice and a husband's blindness, gives the talk its weight. The piece shows Balzac the observer of salons at his most polished and ironic.
arms-and-the-man:
George Bernard Shaw calls his play a pleasant one and sets it in Bulgaria during and after the war with Serbia. The introduction in this edition marvels, with some irony, at orthodox critics who found Shaw ignorant of dramatic art while audiences kept coming. In a young lady's bedroom, a fleeing enemy officer climbs in through the window, more armed with chocolates than with cartridges.

Raina, the romantic heroine, hides the fugitive and slowly trades her heroic ideals for the plain truth he tells about soldiering. Her dashing fiancé Sergius and the practical servant Louka complete the upset of every romance. Three acts of wit carry Shaw's case: war is work, not glory, and sense beats swagger.
b09-luther-freedom-christian:
On the Freedom of a Christian, also called Concerning Christian Liberty, is Martin Luther's gentle tract of 1520. Where his other works of that year attack, this one consoles and teaches. It sets out his core claim: a person is made right with God by faith alone, not by works.

Luther holds two truths in tension through the tract. A Christian is a free lord of all, subject to none, and yet a ready servant of all, subject to everyone. Faith frees the soul; love then spends that freedom on the neighbor. The short work became the best known plain statement of Reformation teaching. Its calm tone still wins first-time readers.
ballads-of-a-bohemian:
Robert W Service organized Ballads of a Bohemian by seasons, spring through winter, following a poet in a Paris garret. The contents promise My Garret, The Sewing-Girl, The Absinthe Drinkers, and the death of Marie Toro, mixed with program pieces like The Philistine and the Bohemian. Service had swapped his Yukon gold rush for Montmartre.

The poems sing of models, pencil sellers, domestic tragedies, and gods in the gutter, in the swinging meters that made Service famous. A cozy middle passage, wife sewing and kettle purring, shows his gift for the sentimental scene. Readers who know only the Yukon ballads will find the same storyteller here, working Paris streets instead of frozen trails.
baree-son-of-kazan:
James Oliver Curwood's Baree, Son of Kazan is the third of his animal books, after Kazan and The Grizzly King. His preface answers hundreds of letters from readers of wild life. Americans, he confesses, have gone after nature with a gun, himself with twenty-seven of them. He has learned to know animals as they actually live.

Baree, Kazan's son by a wild she-wolf, is born in the northern forest. The pup's world is hunger, cold, and the law of claw and fang. A lynx, an owl, and a trapper's cabin shape his first year. Curwood refuses to humanize his hero, letting fact carry the romance. The story follows Baree toward his father's old haunts and man's uneasy friendship. It remains a favourite among readers of true-to-life animal tales.
bond-contract-1895-rothschild-morgan:
The House Ways and Means group sent this report to the full House on February 13, 1895. It is House Report No. 1824 of the 53rd Congress. Its theme is the great bond deal that saved the gold store of the United States that year.

The report prints the bond pact in full, with the terms the syndicate took. That group acted for N. M. Rothschild and Sons of London and for J. P. Morgan and Co. of New York. The deal is a core record of how the house lent to states at the top level.
carolinian: Sabatini set this tale in the southern colonies during America's revolt. A young hero faces love and war in old Carolina. The tale moves fast. The archive keeps the book open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-dund: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Dundrennan describes a Cistercian house in Kirkcudbrightshire, founded in 1142 by King David the First and Fergus, Lord of Galloway, for monks from Rievaulx. Its name means 'fort of thorn-bushes', and the house commands a view over the Solway Firth. Queen Mary fled there after Langside, spending her final night on Scottish soil before sailing from Port Mary. The abbey passed to the Crown in 1587, was annexed to Stirling's chapel in 1621, and was long quarried for stone before repairs began in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-mar:
Alexander Martin Sullivan was an Irish politician, lawyer, and journalist, born at Bantry in 1830 and dead at Dublin in October 1884. He drifted into journalism in 1850, becoming the Nation's assistant editor in 1855 and then its editor and proprietor. From 1861 to 1884, with his elder brother T. D. Sullivan, he made the Nation a potent force for Irish nationality, and he also issued the Weekly News and Zozimus.

Sullivan entered Parliament in 1874 as member for Louth and later for Meath, was called to the Irish bar in 1876, and became Queen's Counsel in 1881. As a Dublin Corporation member he secured the site for the Grattan Monument, giving £400 subscribed by admirers while he was jailed for a political offence in 1868. He defended Patrick O'Donnell in his last great case in November 1883, wrote The Story of Ireland and New Ireland, and laboured as a temperance reformer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-dioce:
The early history of Sodor and Man is obscure. The Scandinavian diocese covered Man and the western isles of Scotland, the Southern Hebrides. It took the name Sodor, or southern isles, against Nordr, the Orkneys and Shetland, for the northern isles. Man may have joined Sodor under Magnus Barefoot, in 1098, having earlier stood as a distinct see dependent on Dublin.

When Man became head of a kingdom under Norway, Eugenius III placed the diocese under Nidaros, or Trondhjem, in 1152, and Anastasius IV confirmed the arrangement in 1154. Man stayed under Drontheim until 1458, when Calixtus III moved it to York. Norway's rule ended in 1266, Scotland held the island till 1334, and England followed. Henry IV gave the island to the Stanleys, who held the patronage of the bishoprics, though the bishops never became spiritual lords of Parliament. The last Catholic bishop, Thomas Stanley, appointed under Mary, was recognized until 1568.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-forema:
Andrew Foreman, Scottish prelate of border family, was born at Hatton near Berwick-on-Tweed and died in 1522. His talents marked him out for promotion. Through King James IV's influence, he soon became a prothonotary Apostolic and took on important missions. The king sent him in 1497 with two envoys to conclude the truce of Aytoun with Henry VII, and later empowered him to negotiate James's marriage to Henry's daughter Margaret.

By 1502 Foreman was Bishop of Moray, exempt from Saint Andrews' jurisdiction despite the primate's protest. As ambassador to Henry VIII in 1509, he sought peace for a new crusade. Julius II intended him for the cardinalate, but Leo X made him Archbishop of Saint Andrews and legate a latere in 1514, with Dunfermline Abbey. His eight years as primate brought vigorous administration, the restoration of Dunkeld and Dunblane, and a synod showing zeal for clergy reform, learning, and solemn services.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelica-kauf:
Angelica Kauffman, painter, was born at Coire in Switzerland in 1741 and died at Rome in 1807. Her father Johann Joseph, a mediocre painter, taught her colours early. Before twelve she was summoned to Como by Bishop Nevroni to paint his portrait. Francis III of Este became her protector. Cardinal Roth commissioned his portrait.

She showed aptitude for music, but friends urged her in vain to give up painting. After Parma and Florence, she reached Rome in 1763 for Winckelmann's perspective courses. Meeting English noblemen at Venice, she moved to London in 1766. Her pictures include The Mother of the Gracchi. The Royal Academy elected her an original member. Deceived in 1767 by a stranger posing as Count de Horn, whom she married, she separated. After his death in 1781 she married Antonio Zucchi, settling at Rome, where her salon welcomed Goethe. Sentimentalism helped her vogue, but her works have since declined for weak drawing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ardbraccan:
Ardbraccan, Hill of Braccan or Brecan, is the site of an old abbey, now a parish and village in County Meath, three miles west of Navan. Its abbey was founded and ruled by St. Brecan, grandson of Carthan Finn, first Christian ruler of Thomond, and son of Eochaidh Balldearg, whom Patrick baptized. Brecan, credited with prophecy, died early in the sixth century by Petrie's dating, or after 650 by Ware's, and was buried at Templebrecan in the Great Isle of Arran.

Petrie transcribed his tombstone inscription, found early in the 19th century. The Martyrology of Donegal calls Brecan bishop of Ardbraccan, but the see's founder was St. Ultan, who followed him as abbot. Ultan, famed for charity to children, wrote lives of Brigid and Patrick and died in 657, and his successor Tirechan compiled Acts of Patrick from Ultan's own lips. Ardbraccan was often pillaged between the ninth and twelfth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-audran:
Audran was the family name of four generations of French artists from Paris and Lyons, counting eight noted engravers and two painters. Their work spans the 1600s and 1700s. Some of their plates rank among the finest work of the burin, the engraver's cutting tool. Charles Audran, born in Paris in 1594, studied in Rome, engraved in pure line, and left more than two hundred plates, including portraits and copies after Titian and the Carracci.

His brother Claude the First taught engraving at Lyons and fathered three sons, of whom Gerard became the family's most famous artist. Later Audrans kept the trade alive into the 1700s. Among them were Germain, Claude the Second, and Benoit the Younger, the last of real artistic weight. Prosper Gabriel, a grandson of Jean, gave up art for law and became professor of Hebrew at the College de France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aurelian:
Aurelian, in full Lucius Domitius Aurelianus, was Roman Emperor from 270 to 275, born near Sirmium in Pannonia in 214 of humble parents. He entered the army at twenty, rose fast through ability and bodily strength, and was proclaimed emperor by the army at Sirmium on Claudius's death. He became sole master when his rival Quintillus, the Senate's candidate, took his own life. The empire he took up was split three ways.

Gaul and Britain stood under a Gallo-Roman empire, the East under Palmyra, and Rome itself held only Italy, Africa, and a few provinces. Invaders pressed the Danube, the treasury was empty, and the coinage was ruined. Backed only by the Danube army, Aurelian restored the frontiers, rebuilt unity, and reformed the state in under five years. He was slain before he could enforce a persecution edict, and the martyr acts tied to his reign are judged unauthentic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auxentius-of-:
Auxentius of Milan was a native of Cappadocia, ordained priest in 343 by Gregory, Alexandria's intruded bishop. After Dionysius of Milan was banished in 355, Arian intrigue made Auxentius bishop of the see, though he did not know Latin. Leading Western bishops tried in vain to bring him to accept the Nicene Creed, the orthodox statement of Christ's divinity. In 359 he made many Illyricum bishops sign the Rimini creed, a compromise formula.

St Hilary of Poitiers publicly accused him at Milan in 364, and a disputation held by Emperor Valentinian's order convicted him of error. His submission was only apparent, and he stayed strong enough to force Hilary's departure from Milan. Though St Athanasius got Pope Damasus to condemn him at a Roman synod in 369, Auxentius kept his see until his death in 374. St Ambrose succeeded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany-beyon:
Bethany beyond the Jordan, the place of Jesus's baptism in John's Gospel, is the subject of this textual entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. John 1:28 locates the baptism at Bethany across the Jordan, but a celebrated variant reads Bethabara instead. Most ancient manuscripts of weight support Bethany, a reading approved by Lachmann, Tischendorf, and Westcott-Hort.

Other old manuscripts, the Syriac versions, and Fathers such as Origen, Jerome, Eusebius, and Chrysostom support Bethabara. Origen's commentary argues for the second name. The entry weighs manuscripts and Fathers to settle a single place-name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betharan: Betharan was an Amorite city east of the Jordan, in its valley plain, some twelve miles from Jericho. Rebuilt by the tribe of Gad, it was later fortified by Herod Antipas, who renamed it Livias for the wife of Augustus, and Josephus calls it Julias. Burnt at Jerusalem's fall, it was restored by Christians and became a bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethsan:
Bethsan, or Beth Shean, meaning place of rest, was a city within Issachar assigned to Manasseh, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Later called Scythopolis, it survives as the village of Beisan, three miles west of the Jordan. Its strength kept the Israelites from taking it at the conquest, and it likely stayed Canaanite when the Philistines hung Saul's body on its walls.

Under Solomon it became the centre of an administrative district, and about the third century BC it took its Greek name. The entry follows a strong city from Canaanite holdout to Hellenistic town, with a name that changed with each master.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boetius-egan:
Boetius Egan, Archbishop of Tuam, led Irish Catholics from penal-era hardship toward the relief of the 1790s. Born near Tuam in 1734 to a once-wealthy Galway family, he trained for the priesthood at the Irish College of Bordeaux. He returned to minister in Ireland, became Bishop of Achonry in 1785, and Archbishop of Tuam two years later.

He welcomed the Catholic Relief Act of 1793 with gratitude to George III. He served as a trustee when Maynooth College opened in 1795. One of his last acts signed an address to Lord Camden condemning revolutionary associations, praising the king as the best of kings. He died near Tuam in 1798.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dolma:
Charles Dolman was a publisher and bookseller born at Monmouth in 1807 and dead at Paris in 1863. The only son of a Monmouth surgeon and Mary Frances Booker, daughter of a London Catholic publisher, he was educated at St. Gregory's, Downside, near Bath. He gave it up when the Bookers, publishers into whose family his father had married, invited him to London.

When Joseph Booker died in 1837, Dolman kept the firm going with his aunt Mary Booker and cousin Thomas Booker. The firm became Booker and Dolman in 1840 and finally continued under his name alone. His periodical career began in 1838 with a new series of The Catholic Magazine. His many attempts to lift the Catholic press to a higher standard came to nothing. Disheartened and ill, he withdrew to Paris and died there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-patri:
An entry on Charles Patrick Meehan, an Irish priest, historian, and translator who spent his life in Dublin parish work and historical writing. Born in Dublin in 1812 to parents from Ballymahon, County Longford, he was sent to the Irish College at Rome. Ordained in 1834, he came home soon after Catholic Emancipation lifted legal penalties on Catholics. After a posting at Rathdrum in Wicklow, he moved to Sts. Michael and John's parish, staying there until his death in 1890.

Meehan wrote histories of the O'Tooles of Powerscourt, the Confederation of Kilkenny, and the Geraldines, and a study of the fate of the Earls of Tyrone and Tyrconnell. He translated Manzoni's tale of a nun, a Latin life of Bishop Kirwan, and an Italian history of Dominican painters. Most of his books went through several revised editions, and he also wrote graceful verse and tales for the young.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-mus:
An entry on the Christian Museum of the Lateran, founded by Pius the Ninth in 1854 in the Lateran palace built by Sixtus the Fifth. Gregory the Sixteenth had founded a profane Lateran museum in 1843 and mooted a Christian collection. Nothing of consequence happened until Pius entrusted the work to Father Marchi and Giovanni Battista de Rossi. Marchi took sculpture, De Rossi took inscriptions, and a third section held copies of catacomb frescoes.

Much material came from the Vatican Library hall set apart by Benedict the Fourteenth in 1750 and from the Capitoline Museum. More came from convents, chapels, sacristies, and private collections, with plaster casts where originals could not move. The epigraphy section, ordered by De Rossi, runs from basilica and baptistery inscriptions through Damasan texts, consular dates, dogma, hierarchy, and civil matters, to symbols such as anchor, dove, and monogram. Its prize piece holds the epitaph of Abercius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christine-de-:
An entry on Christine de Pisan, a French poet and historian born at Venice in 1363. Brought to Paris at five with her father, astrologer and secretary to Charles the Fifth, she was reared at court and learned the ancient languages. At fourteen she married Etienne du Castel of Picardy, and widowed at twenty-five with three children, she refused invitations from Henry the Fourth of England and Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

Christine chose to earn her living with her pen in France, and her prose and verse soon won renown. Her contemporaries likened her eloquence to Cicero. In six years, from 1397 to 1403, she wrote fifteen important books, including a biography of Charles the Fifth, a treatise on educating princes, and the Treasury of the City of Ladies. Her long poems include the Book of the Mutations of Fortune and the Book of a Hundred Tales of Troy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clean-and-unc: The distinction between legal and ceremonial cleanness and uncleanness, as opposed to moral cleanness and uncleanness, stands out prominently in Mosaic legislation. Legal cleanness concerns ritual fitness under the Law, while moral cleanness concerns right conduct. The Law treats ritual states and moral states by different measures, and confusing the two misses the legislation's own division.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-constantino-c:
Thomas Shahan's entry follows Constantino Cajetan, Benedictine savant born at Syracuse, Sicily, in 1560, died at Rome on 17 September 1650. While brothers Ottavio and Alfonso joined the Society of Jesus, Constantino became a Benedictine on 29 October 1586 at San Nicolò d'Arena in Catania. Clement VIII soon called him to Rome, entrusting an edition of Saint Peter Damian's works, completed in four folio volumes at Rome in 1606 and after.

Constant, successful research in Roman archives won Cardinal Baronius's friendship. Through Baronius he became titular Abbot of San Baronzio in Pistoia diocese and Custodian of the Vatican Library, holding the latter office under four popes until death. Baronius owed much to him in composing the Annales Ecclesiastici, praising more than once his thorough knowledge of Roman archives. His labours later earned nomination as first consultor of the new college, the College of Propaganda, closing a life spent among archives, editions, and papal service.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cormac-maccui:
James MacCaffrey's entry treats Cormac MacCuilenan, 836 to 908, Irish bishop and King of Cashel. In 900, by descent, he became King of Cashel, combining spiritual and temporal rule over Leth Moga.

The high king, Flann, assisted by Leinster's king, led forces into the Southern Province in 906, meeting Munstermen under Cormac at Moylena, Tullamore, and losing heavily. In 908 Flann returned with Ceorbhall of Leinster and Cathal of Connaught. Cormac, instigated by Flaherty, Abbot of Inniscathay, had claimed Leinster tribute and signified intent to assume the high kingship. At present-day Ballymoon the Munstermen suffered complete defeat, and Cormac was killed. His Irish Glossary, Sanas Chormaic, explains over 1,400 Irish words. Said to form only part of the Saltair Chaisil, also attributed to Cormac, that work has disappeared, or was at best a collection of transcripts by different writers. John O'Donovan translated and annotated Sanas Chormaic, edited by W. Stokes at Calcutta in 1868.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dan:
A scriptural entry untangles the name Dan, which covers a person, a tribe, and places. Dan was Jacob's fifth son, elder son of Bilhah, Rachel's handmaid, and his name, from a root meaning to rule or judge, is read as God's judgment in Rachel's favour. The Bible says little of Dan himself beyond his birth and a single son, Husim, likely a clan name.

Most passages use Dan for the tribe, whose territory and history are then traced, including its northern sanctuary. A second Dan was a city, and a third sense covers other biblical uses. The entry closes with the tribe's most notorious act: Jeroboam's golden calf at Dan, set up to draw northern Israelites from Jerusalem's sanctuary, a lasting symbol of schism in Israel's story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dean:
An office entry defines the dean, from the Greek for ten, as one of a diocese's principal administrative officials. The term first meant a military officer over ten soldiers. It then meant an imperial household official, and in Anglo-Saxon England a local judge for trials of first instance. Saint Benedict's Rule uses it for a monk set over ten others to oversee work and observance.

Monastic usage soon shaped diocesan life. Distant communities gained priest or deacon assistants to the bishop, known by the early fourth century as chorepiscopi. They were subject to the city bishop and able to confer only minor orders. Sections cover rural deans, with delegated jurisdiction set by statutes, custom, or mandate. They also cover deans of chapters, first dignitaries who take precedence in choir, processions, and deliberations and celebrate Mass when the bishop is absent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-detroit-michi:
A diocesan history of Detroit, established 8 March 1838 across the lower peninsula of Michigan south of Ottawa, Kent, and neighbouring counties, an area of 18,558 miles. Its story, as a suffragan of Cincinnati, opens with Jesuit missions. Jogues and Raynbaut reached the Sault in 1642. Menard followed in 1660, martyred the following year. Marquette's 1671 mission at Michilimackinac raised Michigan's first chapel for white settlers.

Cadillac's post of 1700 grew around Saint Anne's church, dedicated in 1701 as the mother church of the region. John Frederic Reze became first bishop in 1833, and later pages list bishops, religious orders, and statistics, from 237 priests and 146 churches to seminaries, colleges, and academies. A Monroe congregation of sisters, founded in 1845 by Louis Gillet, stands out among the orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocletian: A 1913 entry on Diocletian — the persecuting emperor. Thomas Scannell unfolds his fateful reign. His edicts drenched the Church in blood. The tetrarchy was his famous system. The author of the great persecution. His Split palace is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domitian: A 1913 entry on Domitian — the tyrant emperor. Thomas Scannell unfolds his bloody reign. The Christians faced the second persecution. The informers thrived at his court. The bald Nero of the Roman terror. His 96 assassination is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmund-bailey: A 1913 entry on Edmund Bailey O'Callaghan — the New York historian. John T. Driscoll honors his famous Documents. His pen chronicled the colonial age. The scholars mine his learned tomes. The annalist of the Dutch colony. His fifteen volumes are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-colema: This 1913 reference article on Edward Coleman — the Popish Plot victim. George Hind unfolds his tragic death. Oates's lies condemned the innocent man. Tyburn saw the judicial murder. The martyr of the perjured plot. His 1678 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emmanuel-maig: This 1913 reference article on Emmanuel Maignan — the Minim scientist. William Fox honors his famous Cursus. His mind spanned the physical world. The order prized its learned son. The physicist of the Roman Minims. His 1648 Cursus is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-abram-: A 1913 entry on Abram Ryan — the poet-priest of the South. Hannis Taylor honors his famous Conquered Banner. His verse mourned the fallen cause. The South prized its laureate priest. The bard of the Confederate memory. His 1865 Banner is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-mag: A 1913 entry on Ferdinand Magellan — the circumnavigator. Otto Hartig unfolds his famous voyage. His ships rounded the stormy cape. The Pacific knew the daring prow. The first to girdle the globe. His 1521 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-pere: A 1913 entry on Fernán Pérez de Guzmán — the Castilian chronicler. Jeremiah Ford honors his famous Generaciones. His pen sketched the noble line. The court prized its learned lord. The Froissart of the Castilian kings. His 1450s chronicle is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-firmilian: This 1913 reference piece on Firmilian — the Cappadocian bishop. John Chapman honors his famous letter. He stood with the great Cyprian. The East knew its learned prelate. The friend of the Carthaginian martyr. His 256 letter is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-kerna: This 1913 reference article on Francis Kernan — the New York senator. Thomas Kernan honors his famous career. The entry preserves his modest fame. His state knew the Catholic leader. A statesman of the nineteenth century. His 1892 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-moyla: A 1913 entry on Francis Moylan — the Bishop of Cork. Edward D'Alton honors his fearless rule. He founded the Presentation's schools. The faithful bless the holy name. The prelate of the penal age. His 1815 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-patri: This 1913 reference article on Cardinal Moran — the Archbishop of Sydney. Denis O'Haran honors his long primacy. He shepherded the Australian flock. The sacred college knew its Irish son. The primate of the southern Church. His 1884 red hat is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-tregi: This 1913 reference article on Francis Tregian — the Cornish recusant. Edwin Burton honors his steadfast faith. He suffered for the harboring of priests. The entry preserves his blessed memory. A gentleman among the confessors. His 1608 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-zur: This 1913 reference article on Zurbarán — the monk-painter of Seville. Gaston Sortais honors his famous habits. His brush clothed the Carthusian white. Spain knew its austere master. The Velázquez of the religious orders. His 1664 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gelasius-o-cu: A 1913 entry on Gelasius O'Cullenan — the Irish martyr. The entry honors his blessed death. He died for the persecuted faith. The faithful keep his memory. A priest among the Irish martyrs. His 1580 martyrdom is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-michae: This 1913 reference piece on Wittman — the Bishop of Ratisbon. Michael Ott honors his holy rule. He shepherded the Bavarian flock. The entry preserves his modest fame. A prelate of the nineteenth century. His 1833 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-schnee: A 1913 entry on Gerard Schneeman — the Jesuit theologian. Francis Xavier Delany honors his famous works. His pen served the Roman schools. The order prized its learned son. A doctor among the controversialists. His 1885 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-card: A 1913 entry on Cardano — the Milanese sage. Henry Brock honors his famous Ars Magna. His math solved the cubic lore. The age hailed the daring mind. The father of the modern algebra. His 1576 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-godfrey-goodm: This 1913 reference article on Goodman — the Bishop of Gloucester. Andrew MacErlean notes his famous see. The entry preserves his modest fame. His rule served the seventeenth century. A prelate of the Stuart age. His 1656 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gordian: A 1913 entry on Gordian — a martyr of note. Thomas Scannell records his passion. The entry preserves his modest fame. His blood sealed the ancient faith. A saint of the Roman Church. His 3rd-century passion is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gran: This 1913 reference article on Gran — Esztergom, the Hungarian primacy. Antal Aldásy gives its ancient story. Its archbishops guard the Danube's flock. The basilica crowns the old town. The see of the Magyar primates. Its 1000 archdiocese is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gratian: A 1913 entry on Gratian — the Christian emperor. Thomas Scannell unfolds his fateful reign. He favored the Catholic cause. The West knew the youthful lord. The Theodosius's western colleague. His 383 death is famed. His Milan altar is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guillaume-ren: A 1913 entry on Meignan — the Cardinal of Tours. Ewan Macpherson notes his famous red hat. The entry preserves his modest fame. His house served the nineteenth century. A prelate among the exegetes. His 1896 death is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-fitzala: This 1913 reference piece on Fitzalan — the Earl of Arundel. Edwin Burton notes his famous house. The entry preserves his modest fame. His line served the Tudor age. A noble of the Catholic peers. His 1580 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-glarean: A 1913 entry on Glarean — the Swiss humanist. Otto Hartig honors his famous works. His pen served the learned schools. The scholars prized the mighty tomes. The Erasmus's Swiss colleague. His 1563 death is famed. His 1547 Dodecachordon is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herbert-vaugh: A 1913 entry on Vaughan — the Cardinal of Westminster. John Snead-Cox unfolds his mighty primacy. He built the London cathedral. The missions bless the fearless name. The Manning's great successor. His 1903 death is famed. His 1892 red hat is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hyderabad-dec: This 1913 reference article on Hyderabad-Deccan — the Indian diocese. Ugo Maria Pezzoni tells its Deccan tale. Its bishops serve the southern flock. The entry preserves its modest record. A see of the Indian south. Its 1851 vicariate is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ispahan: A 1913 entry on Ispahan — the Persian city, now a titular see. Siméon Vailhé notes its storied past. Its bishops grace the old lists. The Church keeps its ancient name. A see of the Persian land. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-andrew-: This 1913 reference article on Corcoran — the American theologian. James Loughlin honors his famous works. His pen taught the seminary schools. The Church prized its learned son. A doctor among the controversialists. His 1889 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-clarenc: This 1913 reference piece on Mangan — the Irish poet. Blanche Mary Kelly honors his famous verses. His muse sang the Erin's woe. The nation bless the gifted name. The bard of the famine's years. His 1849 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-macgeog: A 1913 entry on MacGeoghegan — the Irish historian. Edward D'Alton honors his famous Histoire. His pen chronicled the Erin's woes. The exiles prized the learned tome. The scholars mine his vivid pages. His 1764 death is famed. His 1764 Irish history tome is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-japan: This 1913 reference piece on Japan — the island empire's Church. Balette and Ligneul tell the mission tale. Xavier sowed the Kyushu seed. The martyrs bloodied the Nagasaki soil. The vicars guard the rising flock. Its 1912 missions are famed. Its 1912 vicariates are famed.

chronicle-of-the-conquest-of-granada-fro:
Washington Irving wrote Chronicle of the Conquest of Granada as a romantic history of the war that ended Moorish rule in Spain. Irving presents the tale as drawn from manuscripts by Fray Antonio Agapida, a fictional monkish chronicler. The scene is the kingdom of Granada in the late fifteenth century. Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile demand tribute, then turn to open war.

Campaigns unfold fortress by fortress across Andalusia. Readers follow the fall of Alhama, the battle of Lucena, and the capture of King Boabdil. Sieges of Ronda and other strongholds fill the middle chapters. Rival sultanas feud inside the Alhambra, Granada's palace court. Irving blends documented events with legend and chivalric color, giving English readers a vivid, partisan picture of Spain's last Muslim kingdom.
chymische-hochzeit-1616-german:
Johann Valentin Andreae published The Chemical Wedding of Christian Rosencreutz in German at Strasbourg in 1616. It is the third of the founding Rosicrucian texts, after the Fama and Confessio. Where they announce, the Wedding narrates: seven days of allegory in which the aged Rosencreutz attends a royal wedding at a wondrous castle.

Trials, pageants, deaths, and resurrections fill the seven days. Alchemy supplies the imagery, but the book reads like a dream romance. Andreae later called it a youthful jeu d'esprit, a jest that the world took in earnest. The first edition of 1616 stands at the head of Rosicrucian literature. Its strangeness has never stopped readers from seeking keys to it.
count-julian:
Walter Savage Landor's tragedy Count Julian, printed in the 1812 John Murray edition, dramatizes the fall of Visigothic Spain. Count Julian, governor of Ceuta, turns against King Roderigo after the king's dishonor of his daughter, whom Landor's preface insists on calling Covilla, not the ballads' Florinda. Julian treats with Muza and Tarik, the Moorish commanders, and opens Spain to invasion. Opas and Queen Egilona complete a court rotting from its throne.

Landor writes the betrayal as a tragedy of injured honor rather than simple treason. Julian's wrong is real, and his revenge destroys a nation to pay for it. Roderigo falls from pleasure to penitence too late to save his crown. The verse keeps Landor's severity: short scenes, hard speeches, no romance padding. Readers interested in the last Gothic king will find a stern early Landor here, already the prose master's equal in compression.

doe-osti-3930934-commercial-building-con: New office buildings, stores, and warehouses cost what they cost — but why? Deru and colleagues analyze commercial building construction costs, breaking down where the money goes. The analysis helps owners, builders, and policymakers budget with open eyes.
dr-jonathan:
Winston Churchill's Dr. Jonathan is a play in three acts, written during the war and, his preface says, declined by several managers. Churchill argues its theme is now the more timely. The true issue of the war, he writes, was self-determination. Industrial democracy is the twentieth century's watchword, as political democracy was before it.

Act one opens in the library of Asher Pindar's house at Foxon Falls, a New England village the Pindars have ruled for three generations. Pindar owns the mills; Dr. Jonathan, returned from the war, brings the new doctrine home. The drama sets labour and capital talking in one room. Churchill the novelist turned preacher-playwright, certain that economic power is political power. The play was published to be read when the stage refused it. Its Foxon Falls is his fictional America in miniature: a mill, a family, and a reckoning.
epicoene-or-the-silent-woman:
Ben Jonson's comedy Epicoene, or The Silent Woman, first staged in 1609, opens before this edition's long critical life of the poet. Morose, a rich old bachelor, hates noise so much he banishes bells and street music from his street. His one wish is a silent wife, and his nephew Dauphine presents Epicoene, a bride who seems blessedly mute. Truewit and Clerimont watch the trap being baited.

Inside the play, the wedding fills Morose's house with drums, fiddles, talkative ladies, and a bride who suddenly finds a very loud voice. Jonson builds the torment scene by scene until the husband begs for divorce at any price. The final reveal, that Epicoene is a boy in disguise, springs the plot's lock. Readers get Jonson's most engineered comedy, a machine of humours in which every character's ruling folly, silence, chatter, vanity, or greed, is wound up and let go at once.
essays-from-the-guardian:
Walter Pater's short critical pieces are gathered in Essays from 'The Guardian', reviews he wrote anonymously for a church newspaper and later collected by his editors. The volume in Macmillan's 1910 Library Edition prints nine essays on books and writers of Pater's own day. Subjects include Amiel's Journal Intime, Browning's poetry, and Mrs. Humphry Ward's novel Robert Elsmere. A review of Wordsworth's poems and pieces on modern French writing fill out the set.

Inside, Pater reviews as he writes everything: slowly, musically, and by impressions weighed like evidence. A book's merit, for him, lies in the quality of the mind it reveals and the pleasure of its style. The Guardian's respectable readers got aesthetic criticism in disguise, doctrine smuggled in as book chat. Readers curious about Pater beyond The Renaissance will find his working method here in miniature, each short essay a small, exact act of attention.
fama-fraternitatis-confessio-1615-german:
The Fama Fraternitatis and the Confessio are the two founding manifestos of Rosicrucianism. This Frankfurt edition of 1615 prints them together in their original German. Addressed to the learned of Europe, the pamphlets announce a secret fraternity of adepts, founded by Christian Rosencreutz, ready to reform the world.

The Fama tells the founder's life and the discovery of his vault. The Confessio speaks in a bolder, more prophetic voice about the coming age. Together they ignited the Rosicrucian furore, a storm of pamphlets for and against across the seventeenth century. No fraternity ever answered the call in person. The manifestos remain the movement's charter and its enduring mystery.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: FBI interviews from January 2001 collected for the 9/11 Commission. The hijackers were already inside the United States. These pages preserve those interviews. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.

The year the world changed opened quietly in FBI files from January 2001, later gathered for the 9/11 Commission. No one knew what was coming. This file holds that month's material. Its pages add to the record of the past.

FBI investigative material from January 2002 gathered for the commission. The commission itself was newly formed. These pages preserve that record. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.

FBI investigation records from January 2003 for the 9/11 Commission. The new year's inquiry pressed forward. This file holds that material. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
from-the-caves-and-jungles-of-hindostan:
Helena Petrovna Blavatsky's From the Caves and Jungles of Hindostan began as letters to the Russian Messenger, written during 1879 and 1880 and translated here from Russian. Blavatsky warns readers herself that she never meant the book as a scientific work, preferring that it be judged as a romance of travel.

The letters describe Indian caves, jungles, temples and encounters on the road, grouping and colouring true incidents for artistic effect where the author judged it necessary. Blavatsky's translator adds that the manuscript was often incorrect or obscure, and that Indian names taxed the Russian compositors. Readers interested in Victorian India, or in the early writings of the theosophical movement's founder, will find the book lively, partisan and frankly self-aware.
further-adventures-of-the-amateur-cracks: Further Adventures of the Amateur Cracksman, E. W. Hornung's Raffles tales. More of the thief. This book preserves that collection. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
god-s-country-and-the-woman:
James Oliver Curwood's God's Country—And the Woman opens at the top end of the world. Philip Weyman paddles south from the Arctic, singing, after two years along its rim. His partner Radisson has just died of the Red Death after a month's struggle. Fort Churchill lies four hundred miles east and the nearest rail six hundred south.

Weyman travels the Dubawnt waterways alone toward Prince Albert and home. No white man lives within a hundred and fifty miles of his route. The woman of the title waits where the wilderness meets settlement. Curwood mixes canoe travel, loneliness, and romance in his northern manner. A white man's sanity, he says, multiplies itself in the silence. The novel follows Weyman out of the ice country into love, danger, and the claims of the past he left behind.
gomara-historia-cortes-1560-italian:
Francisco López de Gómara published his Historia de Mexico in 1552 as the life and deeds of Hernán Cortés. Gómara served as Cortés's chaplain and historian, and his book became the official story of the conquest. The text here is the Venetian Italian translation of 1560, Historia di don Ferdinando Cortes, since no public-domain English translation exists.

Gómara writes with polish and pride, shaping scattered reports into a hero's tale. Bernal Díaz, who had fought in the ranks, wrote his True History largely to correct this book. Read together, the two works let one watch a legend being made and challenged. Gómara's version, for all its gloss, fixed the conquest's story for centuries of readers.
good-indian:
B M Bower's Good Indian, published in 1912, gathers the Hart family at the Peaceful Hart ranch, where the foundling Grant, called Good Indian, has grown up between two worlds. The contents promise a Christmas angel, claim-jumpers, shots from the rim-rock, and the telegraph operator Georgie Howard. Evadna Hart and Grant circle each other through the early chapters.

Peppajee Jim, an old Shoshone lying in his wikiup, holds knowledge the ranch needs, and somebody shoots Saunders. Bower mixes ranch comedy, a land mystery, and romance while questioning the easy prejudices of her white characters. Good Indian's divided loyalty gives the novel more weight than most magazine Westerns of its year, and its Idaho setting is closely observed.
govdocs-archive_org-TheAcademicSermonsAq:
Thomas Aquinas preached as well as wrote, and some of his sermons were delivered in university settings to students and fellow scholars. The Academic Sermons gathers those addresses in English, as volume 11 of the Fathers of the Church: Mediaeval Continuation series.

In these sermons Aquinas takes a short scriptural text and builds a careful, ordered teaching from it, the same structured mind seen in his famous Summa. The subjects are matters of faith and the moral life, treated for listeners trained in theology. The volume lets readers meet Aquinas the preacher, not only Aquinas the system builder.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AndersonJack-Wa: nsia-AndersonJack-WashingtonPost: the made public government document - Jack Anderson of the Washington Post, Saban Productions material. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FoxSylvan_Fox_S:
Sylvan Fox wrote in a newspaper article dated November 22, 1966 that a new probe of the Kennedy assassination was necessary. Fox had standing to say so: he wrote The Unanswered Questions About President Kennedy's Assassination, an early book of doubt. His article appeared exactly three years after the shooting.

By 1966, criticism of the Warren Report had grown from whispers into a publishing wave. Fox argued the official answers left too much unresolved to stand. His piece, carried by the Newspaper Enterprise Association, brought that argument to ordinary newspaper readers on the anniversary itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HoustonAlan_Hou:
Alan Houston reviewed Gerald Posner's book Case Closed, published by Random House. Posner's subtitle states his verdict plainly: Lee Harvey Oswald and the Assassination of John F. Kennedy. The book argued that Oswald acted alone and that the case against him was complete.

Few assassination books landed harder in the 1990s. Posner answered the conspiracy literature point by point, and reviewers had to take a side. Houston's review preserves one critic's judgment on the strongest statement of the lone-gunman case, written for readers deciding whether the debate was truly closed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MackenzieAngusv: Angus Mackenzie filed this legal complaint against the Central Intelligence Agency and other defendants. Mackenzie was a journalist who wrote about the CIA and fought the agency over information. A complaint opens a lawsuit: it names the parties and states the claims the court is asked to decide. The file preserves his complaint under its case heading, but the evidence here does not give its date or the specific claims it pleaded.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MailerNorman_Ma:
Random House issued 'Books and Bookpeople,' its seasonal catalog, for the summer of 1995. The catalog lists the publisher's coming books for booksellers and reviewers. Among the titles it features is 'Norman Mailer and the KGB Tapes,' tied to Mailer's work on Lee Harvey Oswald.

Publisher catalogs are sales tools, but they also fix a season's ambitions in print. This one shows a major house presenting an Oswald book as a headline title thirty-two years after the assassination. The entry for each book gives its pitch, its author, and its place in the list. The catalog preserves how the book trade framed the case for the fall's readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McDonaldIan_McD: A letter dated February 7, 1974 reached Harold Weisberg from Chevy Chase, Maryland. It discusses Dan Rather's CBS report on a DIA link, the kind of intelligence connection assassination researchers traded as news. The letter also carries personal news from the writer. Beyond the date, the place, and those two subjects, the file identifies neither the writer nor the report's details.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MooreDan_Moore_:
A memorandum dated November 1, 1963 surveys extremist activity in Georgia. It covers efforts to have J. B. Stoner disbarred. Stoner was a segregationist lawyer known for racist organizing. The memo also includes informer reports on the King organization, and related matters from the state's political fringe.

Three weeks later, President Kennedy was killed, and memos like this one were read in a new light. At the time it was routine intelligence paper: who was organizing, who was informing, who might turn violent. The informer reports on King's circle show how closely the movement was watched from inside. The document preserves the names and concerns of Georgia's watchers just before the assassination changed their work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PoolNathan_Pool:
Belford Lawson of the House Select Committee on Assassinations staff wrote this memorandum on January 12, 1977. It went to Robert K. Tanenbaum, the committee's deputy chief counsel. Lawson records an untaped telephone interview of January 10, 1977, with Nathan Pool. The talk covered the 'magic bullet' and Parkland Memorial Hospital, among other subjects.

Because the call was untaped, this memo is the only record of it. Committee lawyers worked the phones constantly, testing witnesses before deciding whom to call formally. Pool's views on the single-bullet question and the hospital were worth two pages of a staffer's time. The memo shows the inquiry's middle layer: not hearings, but the calls that decided what the hearings would ask.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RamirezAntuloAk:
The FBI wrote this letter to Harold Weisberg on October 13, 1981, answering his freedom-of-information appeal. The bureau released 817 pages to him. The pages came from the Dallas and New Orleans field office files on the Kennedy assassination. The release followed a Justice Department review of his appeal.

Eight hundred pages at a time was how the Oswald file reached the public: not by opening an archive, but by lawsuit and appeal. Weisberg's appeals forced reviews that first requests had failed. This letter is the bureau's formal notice of one such win. It preserves the count, the offices, and the date, the bookkeeping of disclosure in a case where disclosure was never volunteered.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SmithMerriman_S:
Merriman Smith wrote this column for the Washington Post's Outlook section on Sunday, November 20, 1966. Its title is 'Dallas 'Exposes' Deflated.' Smith was the dean of the White House correspondents and a wire-service reporter who had been in the Dallas motorcade. He was also a marksman. He writes that he heard just three shots, and he scoffs at the idea of a 'monstrous plot.'

Smith's authority was personal: he had been there, close behind the president's car, and he had handled rifles all his life. His column answers the first wave of Warren Report critics from that ground. Three shots, heard by an eyewitness who knew gunfire, is his whole case. The column preserves the establishment press's defense of the official story, in the voice of its most decorated reporter.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_afghanis:
