In December 1979 the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan, starting a ten-year war. The Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan, 1979 tests two famous claims about that decision in its subtitle: that it served a war on terror, or a drive for warm-water ports.

The briefing book answers with declassified records from the Soviet side and the American side. Brezhnev's government, the records suggest, acted from fear of losing a client state, not from a grand plan. The documents let readers replace slogans about the invasion with the paper trail the decision actually left behind.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_Th: The CIA and Chile: Anatomy of an Assassination - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
A court judgment against a Colombian paramilitary rested in part on declassified documents, and Michael Evans edited this briefing book, number 778, about them in October 2021. The court reached a striking finding about how the fighters related to the state.

Paramilitaries, the court found, had a symbiotic relationship with Colombian state actors. That phrase means each side fed the other, rather than the gunmen acting wholly on their own. The documents matter because they helped a court say so on the record. Readers can see how secret files become legal proof years after the events.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub: Sixty years on, the Cuban Missile Crisis cover-up: the National Security Archive's briefing-book capture of made-public records. What was hidden about those thirteen days. A single capture, dated. From the archive set.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
In May 2021 a ransomware attack shut down the Colonial Pipeline, a major fuel line on the American East Coast. This Cyber Vault posting, dated May 12, 2021, responded within days. Its title insists the episode was not a drill.

The attack, the posting argues, exposed deep cracks in America's digital armor. A criminal intrusion could cut fuel supplies to millions of people, which moved ransomware from an IT problem to a national security one. The record captures that shift in thinking as it happened, in the week the pipeline went down. The week supplied the proof in public, not in a classified annex.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
Under President Richard Nixon, White House aides drafted a blueprint for expansive surveillance of domestic protest movements. John Prados and Luke A. Nichter edited this briefing book, posted in June 2020. Portions of that long-secret plan had just been released, more than fifty years after drafting.

The plan became infamous when it surfaced in the 1970s investigations of intelligence abuses. It proposed watching Americans for their politics, using the machinery of national security at home. Released portions let readers see the scheme in its authors' own words. The record shows how a plan once treated as unthinkable was, briefly, official paper.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
Civilian control of nuclear war plans proved harder in practice than in principle. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 694, published in January 2020. A declassified Joint Chiefs document shows the chiefs wanted to keep Defense Secretary Melvin Laird out of the loop on war plans.

During Nixon's trip to China, the Joint Chiefs sent a message about targeting Beijing's nuclear forces. Laird, angered by its timing and implications, ordered the message recalled. The episode is a small, perfect case of the oversight problem: the civilian secretary learned of a move touching nuclear targeting after it was sent, and had to pull it back personally.

In the late 1950s the United States stationed nuclear weapons in South Korea for the first time, and some of those weapons were huge. This briefing book, posted in November 2019, draws on declassified records of that decision. Secretary of State John Foster Dulles appears in them with a worry.

Dulles feared the hit to America's global political standing if it based such weapons in Korea. Senior Defense officials, meanwhile, pointed to the fiscal benefits of the deployments, since nuclear firepower was cheaper than large armies. The argument between image and savings is recorded in the government's own words, at the start of a nuclear presence that lasted decades.

The Nonproliferation Treaty is now a global standard, but in the mid-1960s it strained the alliance between the United States and West Germany. This briefing book, posted in March 2018, is the second part on the German nuclear question, covering 1965 to 1969. The documents were published for the first time that day.

West Germany had to renounce nuclear weapons in a treaty its ally championed, while Soviet forces sat across its border. Bonn's resistance was about security and status at once. The posting, produced with the Nuclear Proliferation International History Project, shows two staunch allies arguing hard over the rule that still governs the atom.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness:
The Comintern was the Soviet-led organization that directed communist parties worldwide from 1919 to 1943. Corina Snitar edited this briefing book, posted in August 2023, on its Romanian section. Recently unearthed documents from Romania's national archives supply the new evidence.

Moscow used the Comintern to establish hegemony over communist parties in Romania, the rest of Europe, and beyond. A national section's files show how that control worked at ground level: instructions, reports, and discipline flowing between a small party and a distant center. For historians of communism, host-country archives opened after the Cold War remain the richest unfinished source, and this set adds Romanian paper to that record.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Invisib: Guatemala's Historical Archive of the National Police turned twenty with its future in doubt. A National Security Archive briefing book page marked the anniversary under a bleak heading. The heading calls it invisible, silenced, and all but abandoned. Its millions of police records documented civil war security forces and served trials and family searches. Neglect, the heading argues, had become the threat: an archive can be killed by indifference as surely as by fire. Only the page capture survives here, the Archive's anniversary judgment on a prized collection.
hermas-catholic-encyclopedia-chapman:
John Chapman wrote the Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Hermas, an early Christian figure. Hermas is linked to The Shepherd, a famous book of visions. The church once read it almost as scripture.

Chapman reviews what is known of the man and his work. The Shepherd tells of an angel teaching repentance in parables. Scholars debate its date, author, and standing for pages. The entry sums that debate in tight, learned form. It suits readers tracing how the early church sorted true teaching from the flood of visions around it. The Shepherd itself rewards a full read after it.
hofmannsthal-der-tod-des-tizian:
The great Venetian painter Titian lies dying among his disciples in Hofmannsthal's early verse fragment Der Tod des Tizian, given here in German. The Death of Titian imagines those last days as a meditation on art, aging, and passing beauty. Unfinished, the fragment still gleams like a jewel of Viennese aestheticism.

Young artists gather around the master's bed while plague waits outside the villa walls. Their talk circles the question of what art can hold against death. Hofmannsthal wrote the piece in his teens, already possessed by beauty's brevity. The fragment's polish astonishes readers who learn his age at writing. It also opens a window on the whole aesthetic movement of fin-de-siecle Vienna.
john-gabriel-borkman:
John Gabriel Borkman is a play by Henrik Ibsen, here in William Archer's translation with his introduction. Archer notes how little is known of the play's making. Ibsen mentioned it in two letters of 1896, both about his wish to finish a big new work. It appeared at Copenhagen on December 15, 1896.

Archer dismisses gossip that the play aimed at Bjornson, Ibsen's rival, who denied any such portrait. He points instead to a pattern across Ibsen's plays: two women, one strong and masterful, the other tender and devoted. In this play they are the sisters Gunhild and Ella. He also traces the clerk Foldal back to a draft Ibsen made in 1880 for another play.
john-halifax-gentleman:
John Halifax, Gentleman is a novel by Dinah Maria Mulock Craik, in this edition dated 1859. The sample gives its full chapter list, thirty-two chapters in all, without headings. That plain list is all the sample shows of the book's shape. The story it holds is the life of John Halifax, an orphan who rises by work and character.

Craik's hero earns the name gentleman by conduct, not by birth. The novel follows him from a poor boyhood into trade, family life, and respect. Its earnest moral tone made it a favorite of Victorian readers for decades. Readers who want the period's ideal of self-help in story form will find it here in full.
journal-of-an-african-cruiser-comprising:
Horatio Bridge's Journal of an African Cruiser records a United States Navy cruise along the west coast of Africa. Bridge was an officer in the navy, and Nathaniel Hawthorne edited the book. It appeared at London in 1845. Sketches cover the Canaries, the Cape Verds, Madeira, Sierra Leone, and above all Liberia.

Bridge kept the journal's daily form, he explains, because it suited his small literary practice. He mixed in notes from commonplace books kept at the same time. His pages on Liberia, he hoped, would hold readers most. Having seen the colony three years apart, he could judge its progress without party bias, as neither abolitionist nor colonizationist.
jungle-tales-of-tarzan:
Jungle Tales of Tarzan is a set of twelve stories by Edgar Rice Burroughs about Tarzan's young days. The first tale, Tarzan's First Love, opens with Teeka, a young ape, resting in tropical shade. Tarzan watches her from a low branch, devouring her with dreamy gray eyes. No one seeing him would guess a she-ape nursed him as a baby.

His parents died in the little cabin by the landlocked harbor, and the tribe of Kerchak raised him. Later tales cover his capture, his god, a witch-doctor's vengeance, and the battle for Teeka. One story has Tarzan rescue the moon, and another turns on a jungle joke. Burroughs fills the gaps of Tarzan's boyhood among the apes in these linked tales.
kazan:
Kazan is James Oliver Curwood's novel of a northern wolf-dog, published in 1914. Charles Livingston Bull and P. R. Hoskins and Hoffman illustrate it. The contents open with The Miracle, then drive Into the North. McCready pays his debt in the third chapter, and Kazan breaks free from bonds.

A fight in the snow, a wild ride, and a prairie fire carry the middle of the book. Joan, Sun Rock's tragedy, days of fire, and the red death close the list shown. Curwood sets Kazan between the wild and the human world, torn by loyalty and instinct. His northern tales made dogs and wolves into heroes of wilderness adventure. This book is one of his best known.
korolenko-the-blind-musician:
A blind boy discovers the world through sound and grows into a musician in Vladimir Korolenko's beloved novella The Blind Musician, presented here in English. Born into a gentle Ukrainian household, Petrus learns the pipes, the piano, and the songs of blind wandering minstrels. Music becomes his way of seeing, and his teachers include the landscape itself.

Tender and uplifting without sentimentality, the story follows his darkness toward artistic triumph and love. Korolenko builds the boy's inner world from bells, birdsong, and his mother's playing. The novella was among Russia's most cherished stories for generations of readers. Its faith in the human spirit never feels cheap, because the darkness is real. Few books render a sense they cannot use with such care.
lady-good-for-nothing-a-man-s-portrait-o:
Arthur Quiller-Couch first published Lady Good-for-Nothing in 1910. He signed it simply Q. The tale first ran in the weekly edition of the Times.

An American friend suggested its theme to Quiller-Couch. It concerns Sir Harry Frankland, collector of the port of Boston. He loves Agnes Surriage, a poor fisherman's daughter from Marblehead. Their mid-eighteenth-century romance crosses a wide gap of rank. The subtitle calls the book a man's portrait of a woman, which invites readers to judge that portrait themselves. The subtitle warns that the portrait is one man's view. Agnes's patience and worth test that view across the story.
lady-susan:
Jane Austen wrote Lady Susan as a novel in letters. Forty-one letters carry the story, followed by a conclusion. No narrator stands between the reader and the writers.

Lady Susan herself writes with charm, wit, and cool self-interest. Other letters answer hers, judge her, or fall under her spell. Family visits and marriage plans give her room to scheme. Austen's early work shows her irony already fully formed. Readers who know her later novels will enjoy this sharper, colder heroine. The letters let every writer expose a different motive. Austen trusts readers to spot the lies without her help.
lady-windermere-s-fan:
Oscar Wilde's play Lady Windermere's Fan was first published in 1893. Its subtitle calls it a play about a good woman. This Methuen printing went through many editions by 1914.

A fan, a gift, becomes the sign of a hidden story. Lady Windermere believes her husband keeps a shameful secret. A mysterious older woman enters her drawing room and her life. Wilde mixes sparkling talk with real moral risk. The play asks what a good woman owes to truth, mercy, and appearances. A mother's hidden sacrifice sits behind the drawing room comedy. Wilde balances that pathos with some of his sharpest lines.
lands-of-the-slave-and-the-free-or-cuba-:
Captain Henry A. Murray published Lands of the Slave and the Free in 1857. His travels cover Cuba, the United States, and Canada. A picture of a coffee planter's home opens the book.

Lines from Milton and from an anti-slavery song set the tone. Murray insists that God gave no man lordship over another man. The song mourns enslaved people sold away to rice swamps. A Royal Navy officer's travel record thus meets the slavery question directly. Readers get scenery, society, and moral argument together. Murray's naval eye notices ports, trade, and defenses closely. His route through three lands invites constant comparison between them.
last-poems-by-a-e-housman:
A. E. Housman published Last Poems as his final verse collection. In a short preface he says more poems are unlikely to come. He wrote most of his first book in a burst during early 1895.

Housman says he can no longer expect that excitement to return. About a quarter of these poems date from April of the publication year. The rest had waited in manuscript. He printed them while he could still control spelling and punctuation. Readers get a spare, careful farewell from a famously exact poet. Housman's Latin scholarship matched his care over English verse. Every word in these short poems feels weighed and placed.
letters-to-his-son-1746-47-on-the-fine-a:
Lord Chesterfield wrote these letters to his son in 1746 and 1747. Their subtitle promises the fine art of becoming a man of the world. An editor's note explains the old and new style dates.

England still used the Julian calendar, eleven days behind Europe. Chesterfield marked dates O.S. or N.S. to track letters to France. Inside, a father coaches his son on manners, study, and company. Grace, ease, and attention form his constant lesson. These early letters open a famous, controversial course in worldly education. A postscript habit keeps even short letters instructive. Chesterfield corrects his son's spelling, taste, and bearing alike.
letters-to-his-son-1753-54-on-the-fine-a:
Chesterfield opens 1753 wishing his son a happy New Year. More than a fortnight has passed without a letter, he notes. He hopes business, not illness, explains the silence.

Lord Albemarle's bureau fills the son's mornings, he guesses. Evenings belong to business of a genteeler nature, he adds dryly. Two Paris gentlemen lately arrived knew the young man there. Comte Zinzendorf and the academician Clairant are named among them. Work at an embassy now trains the son for public life. Embassy work taught the son how courts really function. Chesterfield values that training above mere book learning.
letters-to-his-son-1756-58-on-the-fine-a:
A letter from Bath, dated November 15, 1756, discusses Prussian papers. Chesterfield has read them with great attention, he tells his son. Courts of Vienna and Dresden stand exposed by them, he thinks.

If courts could blush, those courts ought to blush now, he writes. Armies may soon answer where words have failed, he predicts. Russian power could make that logic too strong for Prussia. War news mixes with family counsel in these years. An older Chesterfield watches Europe slide toward the Seven Years' War. Bath, where he writes, was England's great spa town. Gossip from Bath mixes with news from Europe's camps.
letters-to-his-son-1759-65-on-the-fine-a:
Chesterfield greets 1759 with an Italian New Year wish. Many and happy, he writes, and is done with that lying day. His son's last letter reads like a bill of health, he jokes.

He warns the young man not to presume on good health. Obey and honor your physician, he quotes, for long days. A ribband, some court honor, hangs undecided in the talk. These later letters show a father aging alongside his counsel. The world he taught his son to enter keeps changing around them both. A court ribband could mark favor and future office. Such small honors mattered greatly in Chesterfield's world.
letters-to-his-son-1766-71-on-the-fine-a:
A London letter of February 11, 1766, opens this final Chesterfield group. Two letters from his son arrived late, delayed by bad weather. Roads suffered in one of the severest winters Chesterfield could remember.

Illness spread through London in that hard cold. Chesterfield's own frail body was pinched badly by it. Doctors let his blood twice in four days, with real relief. Age and sickness now frame the old lessons. The series closes with a father's care outlasting his ambition. Bloodletting was still standard care for such illness then. His relief after treatment is recorded with dry gratitude.
letters-written-during-a-short-residence:
Mary Wollstonecraft wrote these letters during a short residence in Scandinavia. Cassell issued this edition in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne in 1889. An introduction begins with her birth on April 27, 1759.

Her father was quick-tempered, unsettled, and sometimes violent, it says. Her mother was a rigorous Irishwoman from Ballyshannon. Against that childhood, Wollstonecraft's travel letters show striking independence. Sweden, Norway, and Denmark pass under her searching eye. She mixes scenery with fierce thoughts on society and women's lives. Her Scandinavian trip was made on business for another. The letters became her most personal travel book.
life-and-death-of-harriett-frean:
May Sinclair published this short novel in 1922 under her own name. Its first pages show baby Harriett laughing at a nursery rhyme. Her mother repeats Pussycat, Pussycat, and the child asks about the Queen. Small bedtime rituals open a whole life told in brief scenes.

The narrative follows Harriett from that cot through her adult years. Sinclair compresses decades into a spare, intense life story. Readers watch early impressions harden into lifelong habits and limits. The novel is prized for its tight form and quiet psychological force. That rhyme returns every evening before bedtime in Harriett's nursery. Her mother enters with a lighted candle, her face between long curls.
life-and-death-of-mr-badman:
John Bunyan wrote this account of a sinner's life and death. A 1905 Cambridge edition, edited by John Brown, pairs it with The Holy War. The volume even reproduces the frontispiece of the Holy War's first edition. Bunyan's portrait, drawn on vellum by Robert White, faces the text.

Mr. Badman's career shows wickedness unfolding step by step toward judgment. Bunyan wrote it as a dark companion to The Pilgrim's Progress. Where Christian journeys toward salvation, Badman sinks the other way. The book delivers Puritan moral teaching at full, vivid power. Cambridge University Press printed the edition at its Fetter Lane warehouse.
life-in-the-iron-mills-or-the-korl-woman:
Rebecca Harding Davis opens this story inside a smoky iron town. Smoke rolls from the foundries and coats streets, boats, and faces. Even a little angel figure on the mantel wears black clots of soot. A caged canary chirps beside the narrator's window.

The tale centers on Hugh Wolfe, a laborer in the mills. His sculpted figure of a starving woman, the Korl Woman, speaks for him. Davis made working-class suffering her subject with unusual directness. The story helped launch realist fiction in America. A dirty canary and a broken angel share the narrator's smoky room. Irish drinkers crowd the grocer's shop across the rainy street.
life-of-bunyan:
The Reverend James Hamilton wrote this life of John Bunyan. Thomas Nelson printed it in an 1845 Puritan Divines edition. Hamilton admits graceful sketches by Southey and Montgomery preceded him. He aims at a simple, coherent account of an unusual man.

Bunyan was born at Elstow, near Bedford, in 1628. His father worked as a brazier or tinker and trained his son likewise. Though extremely poor, the family sent John to school. He learned to read and write there, Hamilton records. Southey's and Montgomery's sketches left few gaps, Hamilton admits frankly. Bunyan's own narrative still guides every later biographer, he says.
lin-mclean:
Owen Wister published these Wyoming stories in Philadelphia in 1897. He dedicates the book to Harry Mercer, its first patient reader. Young Lin McLean wakes in cow camp in the opening tale. He will turn twenty-two during that quiet mid-July week.

Lin could break wild horses better than any camp hand. Only the cook earned more dollars a month than he did. Spring work was done, and fall round-up had not come. Unspent dollars on the ranch books tempt him toward variety. The cook alone was up when Lin woke that morning. Fellow punchers burrowed deeper into blankets against the increasing day.
literary-and-philosophical-essays-french:
Harvard Classics Volume Thirty-Two gathers continental essays here. Montaigne leads with pieces on happiness, philosophy, education, friendship, and books. An introductory note calls him founder of the modern essay. He was born February 28, 1533, at his family chateau.

Sainte-Beuve asks what a classic is in his essay. Renan writes on the poetry of the Celtic races. Lessing, Schiller, and Kant represent German thought in translation. Mazzini closes the volume with Byron and Goethe. Montaigne retired at thirty-eight from public office to study. George Buchanan, the Scottish Latinist, numbered among his school teachers.
maid-marian:
Maid Marian is a comic novel by Thomas Love Peacock about Robin Hood. It opens in the abbey-chapel of Rubygill, near Sherwood Forest. Matilda Fitzwater waits there to wed Robert Fitz-Ooth, Earl of Locksley. The abbot and his rosy friars stand ready, but the earl has not arrived.

Matilda — the Maid Marian of the title — keeps her faith in her lover. Peacock turns the old outlaw tale into witty, sparkling prose. Friars, barons, and foresters debate love, power, and the church. The wedding's failure launches adventure in the greenwood. Peacock mixes medieval sport with sharp modern satire. It is the thinking reader's Robin Hood.
man-to-man:
Man to Man is a Western novel by Jackson Gregory, copyrighted in 1920. Grosset and Dunlap issued it, with pictures by J. G. Shepherd. The hero, Steve Packard, dives into deep waters in chapter one. News of a legacy soon brings him home to the ranch country.

Terry, a spirited girl, meets Steve before breakfast and rides with him. An old 'mountain lion' of a man comes down from the north. Red Creek town, a lumber camp, and a blind man fill the plot. Steve declares one fight his own and will not be held back. Gregory writes of loyalty, land, and old grudges. The tale moves at a gallop to its showdown.
maria-or-the-wrongs-of-woman:
Maria; Or, The Wrongs of Woman is Mary Wollstonecraft's last work. This text follows the edition of 1798, printed after her death. The preface calls it her final literary attempt. Wollstonecraft had already shaken England with her Vindication of women's rights.

Maria is a wife locked away by the husband who owns her legally. In her prison she befriends her keeper, Jemima, another wronged woman. Their stories expose how law and custom cage women. A third voice, the lover Darnford, brings hope and fresh doubt. The novel breaks off unfinished, with sketched endings. It remains a founding cry of feminist fiction.
master-and-man:
Leo Tolstoy wrote Master and Man, here in English by Louise and Aylmer Maude. The tale opens in winter, the day after St. Nicholas's Day. Innkeeper Vasili Andreevich Brekhunov hurries to buy a grove of trees.

He takes church funds to top up his own cash for the deal. His man Nikita, a peasant of fifty, harnesses the horse for the drive. Nikita has sworn off drink, though the feast tempts him hard. Master and man set out into the cold on a grasping errand. The road, the snow, and a night drive shape the tale's core. Tolstoy sets greed and duty side by side in two plain men.
memoir-and-letters-of-francis-w-newman:
I. Giberne Sieveking wrote the Memoir and Letters of Francis W. Newman. A photo from a daguerreotype of 1851 fronts the book. She gave the work to her mother in a short dedication.

Contents move from his forebears to school and college days with his brother. A missionary trip to the East and a Bristol tutorship follow. Long sets of letters to Dr. Nicholson fill the middle years. Later letters to Anna Swanwick run from 1871 to 1887 in the list. A tale of two patriots and a set of reform plans close the book. Newman stands shown as both scholar and restless reformer.
memoir-of-old-elizabeth-a-coloured-woman:
Old Elizabeth's memoir was printed in Philadelphia in 1863. Collins printed it at 705 Jayne Street. Her tale was taken from her own lips in her 97th year.

She was born in Maryland in 1766, to enslaved parents. Both parents were Methodist, and her father read the Bible aloud each Sabbath. At age eleven her master sent her miles from her kin. That loss, she says, left her lonely and sad for a long time. A verse from Galatians heads her tale of bondage and faith. Her plain words were kept as close as print allowed.
memoirs-of-the-life-of-the-rt-hon-richar:
Thomas Moore wrote the life of Richard Brinsley Sheridan in two volumes. Volume one stands here, given to his friend George Bryan. Moore's preface tells how the work was long delayed.

The first four chapters were written near seven years before the rest. A long absence from England held the task in mid course. Charles Sheridan gave him most of the facts on his father. No one but the printers read a line before it was done, Moore says. Moore owns any errors or indiscreet tales as his alone. That candor frames a life of stage and Parliament fame.
michael-o-halloran:
Gene Stratton-Porter published this novel in 1915, with the story centered on young Mickey O'Halloran. Mickey is a small, sharp newsboy who works the streets and looks after his little brother. The opening chapter, Happy Home in Sunrise Alley, shows him bargaining hard with a bigger boy. Chapter titles promise birdsong, miracles, and an orphans' home.

Mickey's world includes wealthier families whose lives cross his own. Stratton-Porter mixes city hardship with her lifelong love of birds and wild places. Themes named in the contents include brotherhood, protection, and second chances. The book offers her readers a warm story of a poor boy's loyalty and grit.
my-native-land-the-united-states-its-won:
James Cox wrote this rich picture book of America for old and young. Its long title promises wonders, beauties, people, tales, and history. Cox had written Our Own Country and books on St. Louis. The volume came out in 1903, thick with pictures.

Chapter one tells the nation's birth and the Liberty Bell. It weighs views of the war and the first Fourth of July. Chapter two turns to the witch of Salem. Court records and grim deaths fill that dark tale. Cox mixes pride, legend, and fact across the land. The book is patriotic show-and-tell from an age that loved big illustrated tours.
myths-and-legends-of-our-own-land-volume:
Charles M. Skinner gathers New England's dark old tales in volume four. Evangeline opens a list thick with hermits and dead ships. Mogg Megone, Father Moody's black veil, and thunder's home follow. Salem and its witchcraft earn their own grim part.

Peter Rugg, the missing man, wanders these pages too. Great carbuncles, lover's leaps, and Howe's masquerade add color. Puritan guilt gave this region a deep stock of ghosts. Skinner tells them with relish for the strange and sad. V1 calls it the perfect book for a dark evening, full of America's oldest and best-kept ghost tales.
narrative-of-the-most-remarkable-events-:
Frederic Shoberl compiled and translated this account of the Battle of Leipzig. The fighting ran from October 14 to 19, 1813. Allied armies met the French in a vast series of clashes. Military maps show each army's moves through the week.

Ackermann issued the eighth edition in London in 1814. A line from Lucretius fronts the book in Latin. It muses on watching great battles from a safe place. Leipzig was the largest battle yet fought in Europe. Napoleon's defeat there broke his hold on Germany. Shoberl's near-contemporary record gathers German reports into one English narrative of the turning point.
nasa-tm-19630012115-a-technique-for-calc:
John P. Sheats and Jon B. Haussler of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this note on September 26, 1962. Both worked in the Flight Evaluation Branch there. Their subject is a method for computing smoothing coefficients. Such numbers clean up noisy test data and find its rates of change.

Flight tests record wobbly numbers full of random error. Smoothing spreads that error out so true trends show through. Differentiation then finds how fast a value is changing. Catalog notes tie the method to flight test observations. Sheats and Haussler gave fellow engineers a clean recipe for the math, at a time when most such work was still done by hand.
nasa-tm-19650018342-steady-and-fluctuati:
Charles F Coe at Ames Research Center measured air pressure on two payload shapes in a wind tunnel for this March 1961 report. The shapes matched the Centaur and the Able V space vehicles. Speeds ran from below the speed of sound to just above it. Both steady pressure and rapidly changing, fluctuating pressure were recorded.

Coe found strong pressure fluctuations on both shapes in a band just below Mach one. Fluctuating loads can shake a vehicle and stress its structure. Knowing where the worst band lies helps designers brace for it. The report gives measured values that later payload designers could use directly.
nasa-tm-19660014568-deformation-processi:
D E Strohecker, T G Byrer, A F Gerds, J H Gehrke, and F W Boulger compiled this April 18, 1966, study of shaping nickel-base and cobalt-base alloys by force. It was prepared under the Redstone Scientific Information Center. Deformation processing covers rolling, forging, and other work that shapes metal by pushing it, rather than cutting it away. Superalloys resist such work by design, since they are built to stay strong when hot.

Shaping them without cracks takes careful heat and pressure choices. A compiled study shares practice across shops and services. Hot engine parts were the main products at stake. The guide served the same Army and NASA builders who appear across this series of materials reports.
nasa-tm-19660016990-machining-and-grindi:
C T Olofson, J A Gurklis, and F W Boulger compiled this April 20, 1966, report on machining nickel-base and cobalt-base alloys. It was prepared under the Redstone Scientific Information Center for the Army Missile Command. The abstract says the report covers the state of the art in metal removal for these alloys. Grinding practice is covered alongside cutting.

Superalloys keep their strength at great heat, and that same trait fights the cutting tool. Tools wear fast, and surfaces can be damaged in the cut. A state of the art review saves each shop from learning alone. Engine builders depended on these alloys for their hottest parts.
nasa-tm-19660020081-radiation-patterns-a:
C M Knop of the Andrew Corporation studied an antenna slot wrapped in plasma. C T Swift at Langley and H Hodara of a California firm joined the work. Their paper was given in Boston in September 1965. The antenna is a long slot cut along a cylinder. A layer of hot plasma covers it during hypersonic flight. The authors report its radiation patterns and its admittance, a measure of how it takes power.

Three kinds of slotted-cylinder antennas are compared in the study. Plasma can block or distort an antenna's signal at the worst moment. Knowing the pattern through plasma helps designers place and tune flight antennas. The work was partly supported by a NASA contract, and it fed the wider study of radio blackout.
nasa-tm-19680010239-experimental-evaluat:
A. J. Pavli, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, fired rocket nozzles to rank heat shield materials. His test used a small storable-propellant engine. Eighteen ablative materials served as nozzle sections across a series of test firings. Ablatives protect by charring and eroding away slowly.

Quartz reinforcement beat silica in the resins tested, thanks to quartz's higher melting point. Carbon-silica reinforcement eroded fastest, because its carbon oxidized quickly. Phenolic resins posted the lowest erosion rates of all. Nozzle entrance angle, throat curve, and resin supplier made no apparent difference. The rankings told engine designers which ablative to trust.
nasa-tm-19680012066-an-analysis-of-aloue:
Robert F. Benson, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, presented this analysis in Norway in April 1968. He studies the plasma resonances rung up by Alouette I, Canada's first satellite. He asks whether the cyclotron harmonic resonances follow the expected harmonic pattern, and how large the excited region is.

Benson reports that the highest harmonics drift from the simple pattern. Their spacing points to a lower field value than the lower harmonics give. Some resonance frequencies shift when the electron density changes. The resonances appear most often when the satellite moves nearly along the magnetic field. Their duration grows with the angle to the field.
nasa-tm-19690010295-global-observations-:
K. K. Mahajan and L. H. Brace of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this December 1968 preprint, X-621-68-506. They present global observations on the thermal balance of the nighttime protonosphere. That is the high region where hydrogen ions rule the ionosphere, sampled here by electrostatic probes aboard Alouette II after dark.

Night electron temperatures formed a trough near eighteen hundred degrees at low latitudes, the pair report. Temperatures rose sharply past three thousand degrees toward middle latitudes. Electron counts peaked near thirty degrees north and south, shifting with local summer. Comparing Explorer 22 readings from summer 1966 showed warmth rising along magnetic field lines. The stored heat, they conclude, needs no outside source to explain it.
nasa-tm-19690022738-preliminary-results-:
C. A. Wagner of Goddard Space Flight Center reports preliminary results from mean element analyses of twelve-hour resonant orbits in this June 1969 preprint, X-552-69-264. Such orbits circle Earth twice daily, in step with its rotation. Their slow drift betrays the lumpiness of Earth's gravity field, if analysts can read the drift cleanly.

Goddard's new program takes short arc mean orbit elements as its data, Wagner explains. Integrating only the slow changes lets it step a full revolution or more at once. Five thousand revolutions then compute in about a minute, and gravity constant effects separate readily. Data from many twelve- and twenty-four-hour satellites, including Molniya and Cosmos craft, feed the analysis.
nasa-tm-19690026875-on-the-interpretatio:
J. I. Trombka of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote part one of this work on interpreting cosmic X-ray and gamma ray spectra. It is dated August 1969 and numbered X-641-69-357. Detectors record a pulse height spectrum, blurred by their own response. The true photon spectrum behind it is what scientists actually want to know.

Trombka suggests that some breaks in a measured spectrum's slope come from the measuring process itself. His method works both ways between true and recorded spectra. One worked example shows a smooth true spectrum emerging from a common crystal detector with several false slope breaks. Undoing the instrument's effects, he shows, also lets data from different detectors be compared fairly.
nasa-tm-19700007986-mie-scattering-a-com:
Nadine A. Bicket and Gilmer A. Gary of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 29, 1969. It covers Mie scattering, the way light bounces off small particles. The pair present a computer program for the math and an atlas of results.

Their program, called MIESCA, works out amplitude functions, efficiency factors, intensities, and polarization. The report first gives background on the scattering theory. It then shows how the results change for different particle groups. It also covers how the lens opening of the light-collecting device affects what is measured.
nasa-tm-19700025051-methods-for-determin:
Samuel L. Miller and David J. Griffith of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston wrote this internal note on January 30, 1968. It gives methods for finding what an orbital transfer takes in near-Earth orbits. A transfer is the move from one orbit to another.

Mission planners must know the fuel and time each transfer demands. Miller and Griffith set out ways to determine those requirements for orbits close to Earth. Their branch, Orbital Mission Analysis, did this work for Apollo-era planning. Sound transfer figures sit under every rendezvous and rescue plan the center drew up.
nasa-tm-19710001888-computer-acquired-pe:
Richard B. Lancashire of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for an October 1970 conference in Miami, Florida. It reports a computer-drawn performance map of a planar diode. The diode pairs an etched-rhenium emitter with a niobium collector.

The diode sat at fixed spacing in a multi-station test facility. That facility fed a central computer system that gathered the data. The computer let the team watch the diode away from its design point as well as at it. Such diodes turn heat straight into electric power. Maps of this kind show where a converter does its best work and where it fades.
nasa-tm-19710002743-acoustic-properties-:
Arthur W. Goldstein, Frederick W. Glaser, and James W. Coats of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a January 1971 meeting in New York. It studies the sound made by a supersonic fan with short blade span. Fan noise was becoming a public problem as jets grew common.

The team measured the fan with and without the stator blades behind it. Those blades let them control wake chopping and other blade row effects. Readings inside and outside the duct told the same story. The pattern of shock waves inside the fan matched the strength of the noise it radiated. Quiet fan design starts with links of this kind.
nasa-tm-19710013187-development-history-:
Clifford E Siegert of the Lewis Research Center traced the SERT 2 solar array in this April 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2246. SERT 2 was an uncrewed spacecraft testing electric ion thrusters in orbit. Its wings held about thirty three thousand small silicon solar cells. The array fed the thruster and the spacecraft systems.

At mission end the array was rated to supply about eleven hundred watts for the thruster. It also supplied about one hundred eighty watts for command, telemetry, and control systems. Design changes stayed small, since similar arrays had flown well before. Flight results showed the array met every mission need.
nasa-tm-19710016272-development-of-an-ai:
Joseph M Sherfey of the Goddard Space Flight Center described a new heat measuring device in this May 1971 preprint, X-764-71-190. The air flow calorimeter balances an unknown heat output against a known one. Sherfey built it to measure the heat given off by spacecraft nickel cadmium battery cells. Knowing that heat helps engineers keep batteries within safe temperatures.

Under set conditions, the prototype measured heat from ten milliwatts up to one watt. Its error stayed within one percent. Sherfey also reported the data plainly. The readings exposed weaknesses in the design. He pointed to changes that would improve the device in clear ways.
nasa-tm-19710016668-apollo-11-lunar-surf:
Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Operations Plan is the final edition of the plan for the first crewed Moon landing's surface work. It defines equipment requirements, crew and equipment interfaces, and the final flight planning for the moonwalk. Its main concern is the extravehicular activity, the work the two astronauts would do outside the lunar module.

The nominal plan covers a single two-man excursion lasting about two hours and forty minutes. A safety red line would end the walk early if oxygen or feedwater in the backpacks fell to a thirty-minute reserve. The plan also lays out three other timelines: one alternate and two contingent versions. The alternate adds deploying an S-band antenna, while the contingent versions shrink the walk to one man, for minimum time or for two hours.
nasa-tm-19710028062-investigation-of-pac:
Clarence O Keffer of the Langley Research Center tested a large inflatable lunar shelter model. The work ran both in open air and inside Langley's large vacuum chamber. An inflatable shelter could give Moon crews living space that launches in a small package. Keffer studied how the model folded, packed, opened, and leaked. A small scale model first set the folding method.

The full model packed down by a factor of about six and a half. Its gas leak rate stayed below a quarter kilogram per day. The shelter opened successfully in near vacuum conditions. After all the packing and deployment tests, inspectors found no real damage. The composite wall structure had survived the handling well.
nasa-tm-19720015252-gravity-gradient-tor:
David J McGill wrote this report on March 22, 1972, as NASA TM X-64651, while a summer faculty fellow at Marshall. McGill taught engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He worked in the Astrionics Laboratory there. His subject is the gentle twisting force gravity exerts on a space station. A long station feels a stronger pull at its nearer end, and that difference tries to turn it.

McGill examined that torque across a full orbit for several station layouts. Two flight modes were covered, called Y-POP and inertial hold. He derived the equations needed to allow for turning solar panels. A step by step procedure follows from those equations. Designers of the modular station could then size their control systems.
new-version-of-les-contes-d-hoffmann-the:
Jacques Offenbach's opera Les Contes d'Hoffmann appears here in a new version, with a book by Jules Barbier. Charles Alfred Byrne made the new English version. Steinway and Sons issued it in New York in 1907. The opera was first given in America at the Manhattan Opera House, under Oscar Hammerstein.

The title page promises an original and novel first act, with other large changes. Both English and French texts are printed in this edition, errors and all, per a transcriber's note. The cast list opens with Hoffmann himself. Counselor Lindorf, Coppelius, and Dapertutto stand among his foes. Singers and readers could follow the whole opera in two tongues.
nobody-s-man:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published Nobody's Man in 1921, a tale of politics and rest. Andrew Tallente, a great statesman, steps off a quaint little train in a Devonshire hamlet among hills. A tall, ungainly man waits on the flower decked platform with an unpleasant smile. The meeting, Tallente sees at once, is no accident.

Miller greets him with a challenge about statesmen needing to leave the treadmill. Oppenheim sets the two men side by side in sharp contrast. Tallente bears heritage, education, and natural culture in his manner. Miller, a postman's son from a small Scotch town, mimics social gifts he lacks. Old rivalry walks off the platform with them.
note-on-the-resemblances-and-differences:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this note on the brains of men and apes for Charles Darwin's Descent of Man. It stands there at the end of chapter seven, closing part one. Huxley takes up a fight then about fifteen years old. The question was how far ape and human brains truly differ in structure.

Some had claimed, again and again, that all ape brains lack certain parts. The parts named were the posterior lobes, the posterior cornu, and the hippocampus minor. Those parts are plain in man, they said, and missing in apes. Huxley answers that all three are as well developed in apes as in men. All primates but lemurs, he says, share them.
noto-an-unexplored-corner-of-japan:
Percival Lowell wrote Noto as an account of a corner of Japan he calls unexplored. A letter to Basil Hall Chamberlain opens the book. Lowell asks Chamberlain to be his best man in the matter before the world. The fancy took me to go to Noto, he begins, calling it love at first sight on a Tokyo map.

Contents trace the road: the Usui Pass, Zenkoji, and a new cornice road. The Etchiu delta, the Arayama Pass, and an inland sea follow. Snow, a genial inkyo, a passport, and a basha carriage all get chapters. Down the Tenriu river and to the sea close the trip. Lowell travels for the love of the place.
observations-of-a-retired-veteran:
Henry C. Tinsley, editor of the Vindicator at Staunton, Virginia, wrote his Observations of a Retired Veteran under the pen name P. Boyzy. An introduction explains that the essays ran at intervals over years in that weekly paper. Tinsley had laid down his arms at the close of the War between the States, it says.

The essays mix winning humor with pathos, the introduction claims. Shrewd, homely wit joins a deep knowledge of the human heart. Political journalism took most of Tinsley's strength until his last illness. These pieces were his outlet for a courageous, hopeful philosophy. To cover pain with a jest, and preach love without cant, was his gospel.
occasional-thoughts-in-reference-to-a-ve:
Damaris, Lady Masham, wrote this discourse on Christian life. It was printed in London in 1705. The preface says the papers waited two years before publication. Friends urged her to share them for wider use. The subject is how people learn virtue.

Masham argues that good principles need early habits. Neither one alone can form a good life, she says. She blames loose education for much vice and sadness. Parents must teach with steady care, she urges. The work links family training to happiness here and hereafter. Her calm tone suits the private, thoughtful form of the work.
on-being-human:
Woodrow Wilson wrote this literary essay before his presidency. It first appeared in the Atlantic Monthly in 1897. Wilson held doctoral and honorary degrees at that time. The essay is divided into six numbered parts. It asks what makes a book truly worth reading.

Wilson quotes Bagehot on the knack of human style. He says readers seek companionship, not mere instruction. Good books widen the reader's world of men and affairs. He warns against tearing texts apart for grammar drills. Leave the text whole, he urges, and read it alive. The essay shows Wilson as a thoughtful man of letters.
on-some-fossil-remains-of-man:
Thomas Henry Huxley wrote this essay on early human fossils. He studies skulls from Engis and the Neanderthal valley. Sir Charles Lyell had checked their geology with care. The Engis skull lay with mammoth and rhinoceros bones. That link gave it very great age, Huxley argues.

Huxley asks if fossils bridge the gap between man and apes. He finds man a well defined group among primates. No living form links man to the next family, he says. Fossils might narrow that gap, but evidence stays thin. It shows Victorian science weighing human antiquity.
one-young-man:
John Ernest Hodder-Williams edited this true war story in 1917. Hodder and Stoughton published it in London that year. The subtitle calls it the simple, true story of a clerk. He enlisted in 1914 and fought on the Western Front. He served nearly two years before the Somme.

The clerk was severely wounded at the Battle of the Somme. He was then on his way back to his desk. The book is dedicated to Sir George Williams. Williams founded the Y.M.C.A. and was the editor's uncle. Chapter one introduces the young man to readers. Chapter two follows him as he joins the army.
our-friend-the-charlatan:
George Gissing's novel Our Friend the Charlatan opens at Alverholme Vicarage, where the Reverend Philip Lashmar waits for a breakfast that is never served to time. Lashmar is in his sixty-seventh year: thin, round-shouldered, and bearded like Darwin. The resemblance pleases him. He lives in ceaseless mild indignation against the age. A newspaper article as depressing as he could have wished privately pleases him too.

His troubles are also financial. The income of his living shrinks with the agricultural depression, his glebe yields less each year, and his small private fortune is nearly spent on charities he refuses to stint. Gissing, the great novelist of genteel poverty, builds the book on such a man: broad-minded in private, contemptuous in public, and worried over everything.
our-mr-wrenn-the-romantic-adventures-of-:
Sinclair Lewis's first novel, Our Mr. Wrenn, appeared in 1914 with the subtitle The Romantic Adventures of a Gentle Man. Its chapter titles track the hero's escape from loneliness. He walks with Miss Theresa, then starts for the Land of Elsewhere. He finds quaint English flavor and encounters the intellectuals. He goes a-gipsying, buys an orange tie, and at last discovers America.

Chapter one explains the loneliness. Mr. Wrenn trots down Fourteenth Street past a dozen movie shows. He wants only the ticket-taker's cordial nod at the Nickelorion. His furnished room is empty, and his daytime job is tedious. Lewis would later anatomize American small towns and Babbitts; here, gently, he begins with one clerk's hunger to be noticed.
paine-rights-of-man:
Thomas Paine published Rights of Man in two parts, 1791 and 1792, as his answer to Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution. Paine had already stirred America with Common Sense. Now he defended the revolution in France and the natural rights of ordinary people.

Part one argues that rights belong to all men by nature, and that governments rest on the people's consent alone. Part two goes further, sketching tax cuts, old-age pensions, and aid for the poor, all paid for by trimming courts and armies. The book sold hugely among working readers and rattled the British state. Paine was tried for sedition in his absence.
paris-war-days-diary-of-an-american: Charles Inman Barnard's Paris War Days is the diary of an American. Barnard was the New York Tribune's Paris correspondent. Harvard gave him his law degree, and France made him a Knight of the Legion of Honor. He dedicated the diary to Ogden Mills Reid. It memorializes Reid's father Whitelaw, the Tribune's late editor. The hosted sample shows the title pages and illustrations list only. Ambassador Herrick fronts it. A wrecked German shop and the American Ambulance Hospital appear. No diary entry itself appears in the sample.
paula-the-waldensian:
Eva Lecomte wrote Paula the Waldensian for young readers, and this English version was adapted and translated from a Spanish one. Lecomte lived at Villar-Pellice in France, among the hills of the Waldensian valleys. Her preface introduces Paula as a simple country girl, tender-hearted and forgetful of self, who loved God with all her heart.

The Waldensians were an old Alpine people who kept their faith through centuries of persecution. Paula's story shows that faith in a young life. Lecomte compares her to a clear brook slipping between flowered banks, and says she conquered by love.
peeps-at-many-lands-japan: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Peeps at Many Lands: Japan, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names John Finnemore as author and Ella Du Cane as the artist of twelve full-page colour illustrations. The contents cover the land of the rising sun, boys and girls in Japan, life in the house, a Japanese day. Games follow, and the feast of dolls and the feast of flags.
personal-experience-of-a-physician: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Personal Experience of a Physician, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names John Ellis, M.D., and promises an appeal to the medical and clerical professions, with an appendix reviewing Christ and the temperance question. The contents move from his personal medical experience to chapters urging physicians to examine homoeopathy, warning of dangers in allopathic treatment, and turning to his religious experience.
peter-pan:
J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan, in the Peter and Wendy text of 1911, begins with a law of childhood: all children, except one, grow up. Wendy Darling learns at two years old, over a flower given to her mother, that she must grow up too. Two, Barrie says, is the beginning of the end.

The contents promise Peter breaking through, the shadow, the flight, and the island come true. In Neverland wait the mermaids' lagoon, the home under the ground, and Captain Hook's pirate ship. The final chapter, When Wendy Grew Up, gives the story its famous ache: Peter alone stays a child.
pierre-and-jean:
Guy de Maupassant's novel Pierre and Jean, read here in Clara Bell's English translation, follows two brothers in the Roland family. It opens on a fishing party at sea, where old Roland grumbles over his line while his wife dozes beside their guest, Madame Rosemilly.

Pierre and Jean sit to port and starboard, each holding a line twisted round his finger, laughing at their father's temper. That easy family scene sets up the contrast between the brothers that drives the book. Maupassant builds the story in nine chapters, watching how money, suspicion, and family feeling can split two sons of the same house.
poems-by-walt-whitman:
Walt Whitman's poems reach English readers here in a selection made and edited by William Michael Rossetti, the Pre-Raphaelite critic who championed Whitman in Britain. Rossetti's letter to William Bell Scott explains his debt: Scott gave him the original quarto Leaves of Grass soon after its first appearance in 1855. When few Britons had read it and most who did found only matter for ridicule. Rossetti read eagerly and found power beyond any praise.

Quotations from Michelangelo, Swedenborg, Carlyle, and Robespierre stand at the front as a guard of honor for a poet England had mocked. The selection itself draws on Leaves of Grass, giving British readers a manageable Whitman, chosen by one of his earliest and most serious admirers. The edition marks the moment American poetry forced its way into English respect.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-madame:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Madame de Montespan selects from the recollections of Louis XIV's famous mistress, set in alphabetical order by David Widger. Montespan writes of the court that made and unmade her, armed, as one entry says, with beauty and sarcasm.

The death-in-life of a convent opens the extracts. Ambition puts a thick bandage over the eyes. Things are always sold at a loss when they must be sold at a set moment. A woman happy with a man who takes her husband's place sketches her own story. "Hate me, but fear me" sums up the pride that runs through the selection.
raffles-further-adventures-of-the-amateu:
Raffles: Further Adventures of the Amateur Cracksman, by E. W. Hornung, continues the tales of the gentleman thief, narrated by his friend and accomplice. The contents list eight stories, among them No Sinecure, A Jubilee Present, The Fate of Faustina, To Catch a Thief, and The Knees of the Gods.

No Sinecure opens with a telegram that reached the narrator in a Holloway attic on May 11, 1897, pointing him to a Daily Mail advertisement. The sender is his rich relative, a knighted specialist who had lately cast him off as a disgrace. The advertisement seeks a male nurse and constant attendant for an elderly gentleman, offering a liberal salary to a university or public-school man.
redburn-his-first-voyage-being-the-sailo:
Herman Melville cast this sea tale as the confessions of Wellingborough Redburn, a son of a gentleman in the merchant navy. Chapter headings tell the story before it starts: his taste for the sea was born and bred in him. He leaves home, sells his fowling piece, and buys his sea wardrobe in town.

Aboard ship he is set to cleaning the pig-pen and slushing the topmast, joins the larboard watch, and turns sea-sick and forlorn. Shipmates such as Jackson, the cook, and the steward fill his days, with a narrow escape and fog work as bell-toller. Ireland comes in sight at last, then Liverpool, its docks, emigrant ships, and dead-house.
reproduction-of-copyrighted-works-by-edu:
Circular 21 of the United States Copyright Office gives basic facts on copying copyrighted works in schools and libraries. The Office states at the start that it cannot give legal advice or opinions on what is allowed. What it offers instead is the text of the law and the record behind it.

The booklet's contents list the exclusive rights section and the fair use section of the copyright law, each with excerpts from the House report. A statement of intent on classroom copying follows. The circular also points readers to the Register's 1983 report on library reproduction, with its seven appendixes of hearings and comments.
rhymes-of-a-red-cross-man:
Robert W. Service, the British-born Canadian poet of The Spell of the Yukon, turned to war in these rhymes, transcribed from a New York edition of 1916. He dedicates the book to the memory of his brother, Lieutenant Albert Service of the Canadian Infantry. Albert Service was killed in action in France in August 1916.

The contents name The Call, The Fool, and The Volunteer first, then The Convalescent and The Man from Athabaska. The Red Retreat, The Haggis of Private McPhee, and The Odyssey of 'Erbert 'Iggins mix battle with barrack humour. A Song of the Sandbags, On the Wire, and Bill's Grave close the list shown, in verse close to the men's own speech.
ridgeway-an-historical-romance-of-the-fe:
Scian Dubh published this historical romance of the Fenian invasion of Canada in 1868, under a motto from Moore: on our side is virtue and Erin. Its introduction is a fiery brief for Irish nationality. Seven hundred years of famine, fire, and sword under English rule, it says, tested the children of Ireland as no other people were tested.

Confiscation, exile, and death were their portion, the introduction argues, yet the crimson ore of their patriotism still flashes. The heart of Brien of the Cow Tax beats in them still, yearning for another Clontarf. Against that background the romance treats the Fenian raid and the battle ground at Ridgeway.
robert-moffat-the-missionary-hero-of-kur:
David J. Deane wrote this life of Robert Moffat, the missionary hero of Kuruman, here in a fifth edition and twenty-fifth thousand from Fleming H. Revell. Deane had also written lives of John Wicliffe and Martin Luther. His preface argues that Moffat's record can never lose interest while noble deeds still stir the heart.

The preface promises dangers faced and overcome: the king of beasts on the African plain, and time spent with chiefs whose warriors' spears had slain thousands. Sickness, hunger, thirst, and years of disappointment stand in the story too. Deane hopes Moffat's strong faith and quiet courage will stir readers, and the young above all, to perseverance.
romano-lavo-lil-word-book-of-the-romany-:
George Borrow compiled this word-book of the Romany, or English Gypsy language, in an edition from John Murray of London dated 1905. Its title promises specimens of Gypsy poetry and an account of certain gypsyries, or places Gypsies inhabit. Things relating to Gypsy life in England fill out the book's scope.

A verse at the front asks, in Romany and then in English, can you speak the Roman tongue and play the fiddle. Borrow states that the vocabulary had existed in manuscript for many years. He had made such word-lists in several countries: his Spanish Gypsy vocabulary appeared in 1841, and a Transylvanian one, made at Kolosvár in 1844, stayed unpublished.
satan:
Lewis Sperry Chafer published Satan in 1909, with a short foreword by C. I. Scofield. Twelve chapters trace a single figure across time. Early chapters cover Satan's career, past ages, and the present age. Later chapters turn to his followers, his aims and tactics, and a coming figure called the Man of Sin.

The closing chapters warn of a grave omission and present-day schemes, then address where believers stand now and how they prevail. In the foreword Scofield urges ministers and church workers in particular to take up the book. He argues that grasping Satan's real power is central to grasping the present age and the struggle each believer faces. The foreword also praises the book as firmly grounded in scripture.
schnitzler-bertha-garlan:
A respectable young widow feels the pull of the bohemian life, and the lover, she left behind. Schnitzler's Bertha Garlan, from 1901 and presented here in English, follows that temptation through a few charged days. A trip to Vienna reopens everything Bertha Garlan thought she had settled in her provincial widowhood.

Schnitzler dissects her inner life with his famous psychological precision, letting thoughts ripple under polite surfaces. Music, memory, and erotic longing mix in her private reckoning. The novella was pioneering work in stream-of-consciousness fiction, before the method had a name. Its portrait of desire against duty stays subtle to the last page. Few writers have entered a woman's daydream with such tact and accuracy.
science-in-the-kitchen-a-scientific-trea:
Mrs. E. E. Kellogg published Science in the Kitchen in 1893, drawing on her work running two cookery schools. She led the Sanitarium school at Battle Creek and the Bay View Assembly school, and she chaired Michigan's food work for the World's Fair. Her book joins food science to daily practice in the kitchen.

Kellogg explains what food substances are and how they act in the body, then turns those lessons into rules for healthful cooking. Many original recipes show the rules at work in dishes she calls tasty and wholesome. Her preface notes that schools of cookery were spreading across the United States, yet most taught clever dish making and skipped the science of diet. Her own Battle Creek classes, tied to an experimental kitchen, ran nearly all year.
selected-official-documents-of-the-south:
Hugh Williams and Frederick Charles Hicks, both of the Library of Congress, edited this set of state papers from the South African Republic and Great Britain. The editors aimed to show, through records, the causes of the war then gripping South Africa. A preface notes keen American interest in the fight.

Williams and Hicks note that the papers sat buried in huge library sources most readers could never reach. They chose a full, linked series while cutting bulk where they could. Students and citizens could thus read the claims, notes, and terms on both sides and judge the quarrel from the record itself.
semmelweis-open-letters-1861-german:
Ignaz Semmelweis fought for hand disinfection in two open letters printed in German in 1861. He addressed them to Hofrath Siebold and Hofrath Scanzoni, two leading doctors who doubted him. Semmelweis had shown that chlorine hand washing cut childbed fever deaths sharply. Vienna's clinics had resisted his finding for years.

The letters lay out his data and his fury in full. They form the primary record of his fight, in his own words. No public domain English translation exists, so the German text stands as a documentary edition. Readers with German meet the scandal of his rejection directly. Medicine now honors what his peers refused.
sermons-to-the-natural-man:
William G. T. Shedd published these sermons with Charles Scribner in New York in 1871. Shedd had written on Christian doctrine, preaching, and the philosophy of history. A solemn preface says the title states the aim: the purpose is to lay open the natural heart.

Shedd holds that law must cut before the gospel can heal, and that his age errs toward softness, not severity. He preaches sin in depth so conscience wakes to its own state. Redemption gets less space than diagnosis here, by design: Shedd saw waking sinners as the preacher's first and hardest present task.
she-and-allan:
H. Rider Haggard first published this African adventure in 1921, joining his immortal queen, called She, with hunter Allan Quatermain. A note in Quatermain's name fronts the tale. Sixteen chapters follow, their heads given as bare numbers in this copy's contents.

Haggard had built both figures across earlier books: the white queen who rules a lost realm, and the plain hunter who tells the tale. Their meeting promises magic, peril, and old African lore. Readers who know either line of tales get a crossing of paths that fans of Haggard had long wished to see staged in full.
showell-s-dictionary-of-birmingham-a-his:
Thos. T. Harman compiled this alphabetical history and guide to Birmingham for the proprietors Walter Showell and Sons. Harman had written a local book of dates and notes before this larger work. Cornish Brothers published it in New Street, with printing by J. G. Hammond and Company.

Thousands of dates and references cover churches, chapels, clubs, schools, parks, theatres, and halls. Friendly societies, charities, colleges, trades, and factories all find entries. Worthy townsmen, population counts, rates, and marks of growth round out the record. Local readers get a full civic portrait of a great factory town in one thick reference.
slippy-mcgee-sometimes-known-as-the-butt: Marie Conway Oemler wrote Slippy McGee, Sometimes Known as the Butterfly Man, printed by the Century Co. at New York. The copyright is 1917, and the title page lists new printings through February 1920. Oemler gives the book to Elizabeth and Alan Oemler. The contents open in Appleboro, then bring Slippy McGee to town, meet the neighbors, and pass under the head Underwings before Kerry enters.
some-mooted-questions-in-reinforced-conc:
Edward Godfrey, a member of the American Society of Civil Engineers, attacks set rules of his trade in Some Mooted Questions in Reinforced Concrete Design. The paper, No. 1169 in the society's Transactions, drew printed replies from seventeen named men, Joseph Wright, S. Bent Russell, and J. R. Worcester among them. Godfrey closes the list by answering his critics in turn.

Godfrey opens with the old art of blood-letting. Doctors once had firm rules for when and where to bleed a sick man, and those rules are now dropped. If they were sound, he asks, why were they left behind? His aim is to show that concrete men hold rules no more sound. Sharp attack, he argues, does good when it kills error, and no reform was ever won without it.
statesman:
Plato's Statesman comes in Benjamin Jowett's English. A first note gives a survey of its thought. Later talks of Plato join two themes in one, the note marks. The Sophist and Statesman show that habit most of all. Their talk serves in part as a show of method. Likenesses come from far off to light the main theme. Stage power falls in the later work as well.

The persons in such talks wake little care. Side paths tend to bury the main claim. The sure Socrates stands withdrawn from view. Plato now fights the sophistry of the schools. That sophistry is making reason itself unworkable. It drives him back toward common sense in his thought. A stress on right sorting marks the late work. Words must not stand in the place of things. Yet the bright ideal is not snuffed out. He still seeks a city of wise kings.
stories-by-foreign-authors-italian:
Italian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, was printed at New York in 1898. It holds two tales by Edmondo de Amicis, A Great Day and College Friends. Fogazzaro's Pereat Rochus and D'Annunzio's San Pantaleone follow. Castelnuovo's It Snows closes the set. Edith Wharton made the English version of A Great Day.

That tale visits a Catholic family near Florence as the Italian army readies its march on Rome. The parents and their grown daughters dread the move and call it the wrong way to take the city, recalling how things stood in forty-eight. Faith, family feeling, and a nation being remade press on each other through the set.
stories-by-foreign-authors-polish-greek-:
One mixed set in Stories by Foreign Authors joins five tales. It holds Sienkiewicz's Lighthouse Keeper of Aspinwall and Bikelas's Plain Sister. Maeterlinck's Massacre of the Innocents and Lemonnier's Saint Nicholas Eve follow. Jokai's In Love with the Czarina closes the set.

Sienkiewicz's tale, in Jeremiah Curtin's English version, starts when the lighthouse keeper at Aspinwall, near Panama, vanishes in a storm, his boat gone from its rocky niche. The post must be filled fast, since ships bound between New York and Panama thread sandbars and fog by that light. Four nations' storytellers share the small volume.
stories-by-foreign-authors-russian:
Russian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, printed at New York in 1898, holds Mumu by Ivan Turgenev, The Shot by Alexander Poushkin, St. John's Eve by Nikolai Vasilievitch Gogol, and An Old Acquaintance by Lyof N. Tolstoi. Constance Garnett made the English version of Mumu.

Turgenev's tale opens in a gray Moscow house where a widow keeps a large household of serfs. Among them stands Gerasim, a porter of huge build, deaf and dumb from birth, brought from his village hut and famed for paying his dues on time. Duels, folk terror, and old soldiers fill out a short shelf of Russian masters.
stories-by-foreign-authors-scandinavian:
Scandinavian, in the Stories by Foreign Authors set, holds tales by six writers. Bjornson gives The Father and The Railroad and the Churchyard. Aho, Goldschmidt, Kielland, and Bremer complete the set. R. B. Anderson made the English version of The Father.

Bjornson's opening tale names Thord Overaas. He is the richest and most weighty man of his parish. He comes to the priest's study to have his son baptized. He names the boy Finn, after his father. Plain farms, parish pride, and family duty give these northern tales their quiet force.
stories-of-red-hanrahan:
W. B. Yeats wrote the Stories of Red Hanrahan, tales of a wandering Irish poet and hedge schoolmaster. The contents list Red Hanrahan, The Twisting of the Rope, Hanrahan and Cathleen the Daughter of Houlihan, Red Hanrahan's Curse, Hanrahan's Vision, and The Death of Hanrahan.

Yeats thanks Lady Gregory, who helped him rewrite the tales in the fine country speech of Kiltartan, close to how the people who remember Hanrahan still talk. The first tale opens on Samhain Eve in a barn, where village men sit by the fire and Hanrahan comes in with a message in hand. Magic, music, and longing follow him on the road.
study-of-a-woman:
Honore de Balzac's Study of a Woman, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's English version, is dedicated to the Marquis Jean-Charles di Negro. The tale takes as its subject the Marquise de Listomere, a young woman raised in the spirit of the Restoration.

Balzac sketches her as a living image of her day. She fasts and takes the sacrament. She goes to balls and operas in fine dress. She holds Church and world together under one motto. That motto is legality. Married seven years to a deputy who waits for a peerage, she stays strictly virtuous, from policy and perhaps from inclination. Balzac warns that women of thirty-six often find they have been dupes of social laws, and watches for her moment of change.
sweet-cicely-or-josiah-allen-as-a-politi:
Marietta Holley, writing as Josiah Allen's Wife, published Sweet Cicely, or Josiah Allen as a Politician, here in its eighth edition, with illustrations. She dedicates the book to the sad-eyed mothers who, like Cicely, look across the cradle of their boys into the great world of temptation and danger.

The preface is a dialogue. Josiah asks his wife a pointed question. Why had she said she loved sweet Cicely best of all her thought-children? She answers that she said it to tell the truth. Plainer still, she said it to keep from lying. Holley's dialect humor carries serious causes, temperance first among them, as Josiah blunders into politics and his wife comments on drink, votes, and village folly.
t-mann-tristan:
A tubercular writer and a Wagner-drunk dilettante circle each other at a Swiss sanatorium in Mann's novella Tristan, given here in German. Art against bourgeois life plays out as tragicomedy of manners around the frail Frau Kloeterjahn. Her husband's healthy world of business has no idea what is happening under its nose.

Mann rehearses, in comic form, themes The Magic Mountain would later treat at epic length. Music becomes both seduction and diagnosis among the patients. The wit here is Mann's sharpest early vintage, cutting in every direction at once. Spinell's triumph and humiliation arrive in the same gesture. The story remains a perfect small specimen of his early art.
tales-of-old-japan:
Lord Redesdale, once second secretary at the British post in Japan, published Tales of Old Japan in an 1910 printing, with the work first issued in 1871. Pictures drawn and cut on wood by Japanese artists fill the book, and the contents mix true tales, love tales, and fairy tales.

Named tales include The Forty-Seven Ronins, Kazuma's Revenge, and The Tongue-Cut Sparrow. A note explains that Redesdale spent years in Japan with the British legation and kept a deep love of its ways. Readers get an early English guide to Japanese lore, codes of honor, and folk tales, still read as a key source.
tallqvist-maqlu-1895-german:
Knut Tallqvist, a Finnish scholar of Assyria, published his edition of the Maqlû series at Helsingfors in 1895. Maqlû means 'Burning,' and the series is the great Assyrian rite against witchcraft. Tallqvist worked from clay tablets held by the British Museum, adding a German translation.

The rite runs through the night, burning clay figures of the witch while gods are called on to break her spells. Tallqvist's edition was the first full printing of the series. It is still the standard public source for Maqlû, since no free English version of the whole series exists.
th-barrel-organ:
Edwin Waugh wrote Th' Barrel Organ, a Lancashire dialect sketch printed at Manchester by John Heywood and in London by Simkin, Marshall and Co. Waugh tells the tale in the broad speech of the moor country.

The narrator sets out from Haslingden town-end with old Rondle o' th' Nab, called Sceawter, a moor-end farmer and cattle dealer. Rondle tells of a cross-eyed cat grown fat by catching two mice at one go, then gives road directions over the moor. Singers are due at his house that night. Readers get Waugh's famed ear for Lancashire talk, humor, and moorland ways, in a tale where the road talk is half the joy.
the-alaskan: James Oliver Curwood wrote The Alaskan, billed as a novel of the North, with art by Walt Louderback. Curwood gives the book, in a note signed at Owosso, Michigan, on August 1, 1923, to the strong-hearted folk of Alaska, a new empire then rising in the North. Chapters are numbered one through twenty-seven with no titles given.
the-amateur-cracksman:
E. W. Hornung's story set, dated 1898 in its heading, brings together eight tales about Raffles, a polished thief who moves in fine rooms. The contents list names pieces such as The Ides of March, A Costume Piece, Gentlemen and Players, Wilful Murder, and The Gift of the Emperor.

In the first tale the narrator returns late at night to Raffles's rooms at the Albany. Baccarat counters, empty glasses, and ash-trays still crowd the table after his loss. He pushes in without ceremony and begs a hearing from a man he hardly knows, though he once served him as a school fag.
the-amateur-gentleman: Front matter and a long contents list open Jeffery Farnol's The Amateur Gentleman, with pictures by Herman Pfeifer; Farnol is also billed as author of The Broad Highway. The book is dedicated to his father. Chapter titles trace young Barnabas as he knocks down his father and sets out for London Town. He buys a prized book from a pedler and meets a lady of quality. He also learns rules for bowing. Silk purses, a fateful lace handkerchief, and a torn bottle-green coat fill out the promised fare.
the-american:
Henry James published The American in 1877, a novel in twenty-six chapters. It opens on a bright May day in 1868 inside the Louvre in Paris. A gentleman lounges at ease on the great round divan in the Salon Carré, head thrown back and legs stretched out.

He gazes up at Murillo's moon-borne Madonna, plainly pleased with his own comfort. James sets a relaxed American ease against the old art of Europe in this first scene. The divan itself, the narrator notes, has since been removed, to the regret of weak-kneed art lovers who once rested there.
the-ancestral-footstep-fragment-outlines:
Nathaniel Hawthorne left The Ancestral Footstep as outlines of an English romance, printed here as an appendix alongside The Dolliver Romance, Fanshawe, and Septimius Felton. An opening note traces how the piece grew. While living in England, Hawthorne planned a romance set in that country, then set the plan aside.

A new idea took its place: a fanciful search for a way to live forever on earth. That idea grew into Septimius Felton and, later, the unfinished Dolliver Romance. The note calls the whole chain a family history of one story. Papers tied to the dropped English scheme still remained after Septimius Felton appeared, and these outlines are among them.
the-beasts-of-tarzan:
Edgar Rice Burroughs dedicated his Tarzan book to Joan Burroughs and opened it with a kidnapping. In Paris, D'Arnot tells John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, that Nikolas Rokoff has escaped from a French military prison. Neither police nor staff agents know how it was done.

Rokoff, Tarzan's arch-enemy, had been sentenced for life on the ape-man's testimony. Contents promise marooning, beasts at bay, a panther named Sheeta, a man called Mugambi, and a dance of death. Later chapters name a Swede, an escape, a trip down the Ugambi, and a return to jungle island and the law of the jungle.
the-bells-of-san-juan:
